'''元伊勢'''は、もともと[[皇居]]内に祭られていた[[天皇]]の[[氏神]]であった[[天照大神]]([[神体]]である鏡：[[八咫鏡]]、と剣：[[天叢雲剣]]＝[[草薙剣]])を、現在の[[伊勢神宮]][[内宮]]に至るまでの間に一時的に鎮座していた場所をいう。
移動は[[崇神天皇]]([[紀元前148年]]-[[紀元前30年]])の皇女[[豊鋤入姫命]]により始められ[[垂仁天皇]]([[紀元前69年]]-[[70年]])の皇女[[倭姫命]]に引き継がれ約60年の間をかけて行われたといわれる。
神体の剣：天叢雲剣は後に倭姫命から[[日本武尊]]に手渡され、最終的に現在の[[熱田神宮]]に移っている。天叢雲剣は、日本武尊が草原で火に囲まれた時、この剣を用いて草を薙ぎ払って逃れたという話から草薙剣と呼ばれるようになった。

'''元伊勢'''は、もともと[[皇居]]内に祭られていた[[天皇]]の[[氏神]]であった[[天照大神]]([[神体]]である鏡：[[八咫鏡]]、と剣：[[天叢雲剣]]＝草薙剣)を、現在の[[伊勢神宮]][[内宮]]に至るまでの間に一時的に鎮座していた場所をいう。
移動は[[崇神天皇]]([[紀元前148年]]-[[紀元前30年]])の皇女[[豊鋤入姫命]]により始められ[[垂仁天皇]]([[紀元前69年]]-[[70年]])の皇女[[倭姫命]]に引き継がれ約60年の間をかけて行われたといわれる。
神体の剣：天叢雲剣は後に倭姫命から[[日本武尊]]に手渡され、最終的に現在の[[熱田神宮]]に移っている。天叢雲剣は、日本武尊が草原で火に囲まれた時、この剣を用いて草を薙ぎ払って逃れたという話から草薙剣と呼ばれるようになった。
なお、この遷宮は一種の軍事行進だったとされている。

'''元伊勢'''は、もともと[[皇居]]内に祭られていた[[天皇]]家（当時は大王家）の[[氏神]]であった[[天照大神]]（[[神体]]である鏡：[[八咫鏡]]、と剣：[[天叢雲剣]]＝草薙剣）を、現在の[[伊勢神宮]][[内宮]]に至るまでの間に一時的に鎮座していた伝承を持つ神社・場所をいう。
『古事記』には伊勢神宮の創始についてはかかれていない。一方、『日本書紀』には、伊勢神宮の鎮座に至るまでに、理想的な鎮座地を求めて各地を転々としたことが記されており、後世の文献にも、同様の縁起が載せられているものがある。 神が旅する説話は非常に多く、『常陸国風土記』の筑波山の話に登場する祖神や民間説話の弘法大師と同じく、「旅する神」の典型的な類型である。一般の神社の縁起でも、鎮座地を求めて神が旅する話は多い。一方、中小クラスの神社が、縁起の中で自社を権威ある大社の古い鎮座地だとすることで、権威付けをすることもあり、「元春日」「元住吉」などと「元～」を称する神社もある。
移動は[[崇神天皇]]（[[紀元前148年]]-[[紀元前30年]]）の皇女[[豊鋤入姫命]]により倭国、笠縫邑に移され、その後[[垂仁天皇]]（[[紀元前69年]]-[[70年]]）の第四皇女[[倭姫命]]に引き継がれ約60年の間をかけて行われたといわれる。
神体の剣：天叢雲剣は後に倭姫命から[[日本武尊]]に手渡され、最終的に現在の[[熱田神宮]]に移っている。天叢雲剣は、日本武尊が草原で火に囲まれた時、この剣を用いて草を薙ぎ払って逃れたという話から草薙剣と呼ばれるようになった。
なお、この遷宮は一種の軍事行進だったとされている。

'''元伊勢'''は、もともと[[皇居]]内に祭られていた[[天皇]]家（当時は大王家）の[[氏神]]であった[[天照大神]]（[[神体]]である鏡：[[八咫鏡]]、と剣：[[天叢雲剣]]＝草薙剣）を、現在の[[伊勢神宮]][[内宮]]に至るまでの間に一時的に鎮座していた伝承を持つ神社・場所をいう。
『古事記』には伊勢神宮の創始についてはかかれていない。一方、『日本書紀』には、伊勢神宮の鎮座に至るまでに、理想的な鎮座地を求めて各地を転々としたことが記されており、後世の文献にも、同様の縁起が載せられているものがある。 神が旅する説話は非常に多く、『常陸国風土記』の筑波山の話に登場する祖神や民間説話の弘法大師と同じく、「旅する神」の典型的な類型である。一般の神社の縁起でも、鎮座地を求めて神が旅する話は多い。一方、中小クラスの神社が、縁起の中で自社を権威ある大社の古い鎮座地だとすることで、権威付けをすることもあり、「元春日」「元住吉」などと「元～」を称する神社もある。
移動は[[崇神天皇]]（[[紀元前148年]]-[[紀元前30年]]）の皇女[[豊鋤入姫命]]により倭国、笠縫邑に移され、その後[[垂仁天皇]]（[[紀元前69年]]-[[70年]]）の第四皇女[[倭姫命]]に引き継がれ約60年の間をかけて行われたといわれる。

『古事記』には伊勢神宮の創始についてはかかれていない。一方、『日本書紀』には、伊勢神宮の鎮座に至るまでに、理想的な鎮座地を求めて各地を転々としたことが記されており、後世の文献にも、同様の縁起が載せられているものがある。 神が旅する説話は非常に多く、『常陸国風土記』の筑波山の話に登場する祖神や民間説話の弘法大師と同じく、「旅する神」の典型的な類型である。一般の神社の縁起でも、鎮座地を求めて神が旅する話は多い。一方、中小クラスの神社が、縁起の中で自社を権威ある大社の古い鎮座地だとすることで、権威付けをすることもあり、「元春日」「元住吉」などと「元～」を称する神社もある。

'''元伊勢'''は、もともと[[皇居]]内に祭られていた[[天皇]]家（当時は大王家）の[[氏神]]であった[[天照大神]]（[[神体]]である鏡：[[八咫鏡]]、と剣：[[天叢雲剣]]＝草薙剣）を、現在の[[伊勢神宮]][[内宮]]に至るまでの間に一時的に鎮座していた伝承を持つ神社・場所をいう。
『古事記』には伊勢神宮の創始についてはかかれていない。一方、『日本書紀』には、伊勢神宮の鎮座に至るまでに、理想的な鎮座地を求めて各地を転々としたことが記されており、後世の文献にも、同様の縁起が載せられているものがある。 神が旅する説話は非常に多く、『常陸国風土記』の筑波山の話に登場する祖神や民間説話の弘法大師と同じく、「旅する神」の典型的な類型である。一般の神社の縁起でも、鎮座地を求めて神が旅する話は多い。一方、中小クラスの神社が、縁起の中で自社を権威ある大社の古い鎮座地だとすることで、権威付けをすることもあり、「元春日」「元住吉」などと「元～」を称する神社もある。
移動は[[崇神天皇]]（[[紀元前148年]]-[[紀元前30年]]）の皇女[[豊鋤入姫命]]により倭国、笠縫邑に移され、その後[[垂仁天皇]]（[[紀元前69年]]-[[70年]]）の第四皇女[[倭姫命]]に引き継がれ約60年の間をかけて行われたといわれる。
神体の剣：天叢雲剣は後に倭姫命から[[日本武尊]]に手渡され、最終的に現在の[[熱田神宮]]に移っている。天叢雲剣は、日本武尊が草原で火に囲まれた時、この剣を用いて草を薙ぎ払って逃れたという話から草薙剣と呼ばれるようになった。
なお、この遷宮は一種の軍事行進だったとされている。

『古事記』には伊勢神宮の創始についてはかかれていない。一方、『日本書紀』には、伊勢神宮の鎮座に至るまでに、理想的な鎮座地を求めて各地を転々としたことが記されており、後世の文献にも、同様の縁起が載せられているものがある。 神が旅する説話は非常に多く、『常陸国風土記』の筑波山の話に登場する祖神や民間説話の弘法大師と同じく、「旅する神」の典型的な類型である。一般の神社の縁起でも、鎮座地を求めて神が旅する話は多い。一方、中小クラスの神社が、縁起の中で自社を権威ある大社の古い鎮座地だとすることで、権威付けをすることもあり、「元春日」「元住吉」などと「元～」を称する神社もある。
移動は[[崇神天皇]]（[[紀元前148年]]-[[紀元前30年]]）の皇女[[豊鋤入姫命]]により倭国、笠縫邑に移され、その後[[垂仁天皇]]（[[紀元前69年]]-[[70年]]）の第四皇女[[倭姫命]]に引き継がれ約60年の間をかけて行われたといわれる。

'''元伊勢'''は、もともと[[皇居]]内に祭られていた[[天皇]]家（当時は大王家）の[[氏神]]であった[[天照大神]]（[[神体]]である鏡：[[八咫鏡]]、と剣：[[天叢雲剣]]＝草薙剣）を、現在の[[伊勢神宮]][[内宮]]に至るまでの間に一時的に鎮座していた伝承を持つ神社・場所をいう。
『古事記』には伊勢神宮の創始についてはかかれていない。一方、『日本書紀』には、伊勢神宮の鎮座に至るまでに、理想的な鎮座地を求めて各地を転々としたことが記されており、後世の文献にも、同様の縁起が載せられているものがある。 神が旅する説話は非常に多く、『常陸国風土記』の筑波山の話に登場する祖神や民間説話の弘法大師と同じく、「旅する神」の典型的な類型である。一般の神社の縁起でも、鎮座地を求めて神が旅する話は多い。一方、中小クラスの神社が、縁起の中で自社を権威ある大社の古い鎮座地だとすることで、権威付けをすることもあり、「元春日」「元住吉」などと「元～」を称する神社もある。
移動は[[崇神天皇]]（[[紀元前148年]]-[[紀元前30年]]）の皇女[[豊鍬入姫命|豊鋤入姫命]]により倭国、笠縫邑に移され、その後[[垂仁天皇]]（[[紀元前69年]]-[[70年]]）の第四皇女[[倭姫命]]に引き継がれ約60年の間をかけて行われたといわれる。

なお、この遷宮は一種の軍事行進だったとされている。

'''元伊勢'''は、もともと[[皇居]]内に祭られていた[[天皇]]家（当時は大王家）の[[氏神]]であった[[天照大神]]（[[神体]]である鏡：[[八咫鏡]]、と剣：[[天叢雲剣]]＝草薙剣）を、現在の[[伊勢神宮]][[内宮]]に至るまでの間に一時的に鎮座していた伝承を持つ神社・場所をいう。
『古事記』には伊勢神宮の創始についてはかかれていない。一方、『日本書紀』には、伊勢神宮の鎮座に至るまでに、理想的な鎮座地を求めて各地を転々としたことが記されており、後世の文献にも、同様の縁起が載せられているものがある。 神が旅する説話は非常に多く、『常陸国風土記』の筑波山の話に登場する祖神や民間説話の弘法大師と同じく、「旅する神」の典型的な類型である。一般の神社の縁起でも、鎮座地を求めて神が旅する話は多い。一方、中小クラスの神社が、縁起の中で自社を権威ある大社の古い鎮座地だとすることで、権威付けをすることもあり、「元春日」「元住吉」などと「元～」を称する神社もある。
移動は[[崇神天皇]]（[[紀元前148年]]-[[紀元前30年]]）の皇女[[豊鍬入姫命|豊鋤入姫命]]により倭国、笠縫邑に移され、その後[[垂仁天皇]]（[[紀元前69年]]-[[70年]]）の第四皇女[[倭姫命]]に引き継がれ約60年の間をかけて行われたといわれる。
神体の剣：天叢雲剣は後に倭姫命から[[日本武尊]]に手渡され、最終的に現在の[[熱田神宮]]に移っている。天叢雲剣は、日本武尊が草原で火に囲まれた時、この剣を用いて草を薙ぎ払って逃れたという話から草薙剣と呼ばれるようになった。
なお、この遷宮は一種の軍事行進だったとされている。

'''元伊勢'''（もといせ）は、もともと[[皇居]]内に祭られていた[[皇祖神]]の[[天照大御神]]を[[伊勢神宮]][[内宮]]に至るまでの間に一時的に祀った伝承を持つ神社・場所をいう。
『古事記』には伊勢神宮の創始についてはかかれていない。一方、『日本書紀』には、伊勢神宮の鎮座に至るまでに、理想的な鎮座地を求めて各地を転々としたことが記されている。後世の『倭姫命世記』などでは縁起が詳述されている。
神が旅する説話は非常に多く、『常陸国風土記』の筑波山の話に登場する祖神や民間説話の弘法大師と同じく、「旅する神」の典型的な類型である。一般の神社の縁起でも、鎮座地を求めて神が旅する話は多い。
移動は[[崇神天皇]]（[[紀元前148年]]-[[紀元前30年]]）の皇女[[豊鍬入姫命|豊鋤入姫命]]により倭国、笠縫邑に移され、その後[[垂仁天皇]]（[[紀元前69年]]-[[70年]]）の第四皇女[[倭姫命]]に引き継がれ約60年の間をかけて行われたといわれる。

[http://www.motoise.jp/main/motoise/index.html 参考資料] （[[倭姫命世紀]]による?）
なお、外宮の元遷座地も元伊勢と称されている。 その比定地として、京丹後市峰山町久次の比沼麻奈為神社、網野町の奈具神社、宮津市府中の籠神社摂社、真名井神社、福知山市大江町の豊受大神社などがある。いずれも丹後地方である。

'''元伊勢'''（もといせ）は、[[三重県]][[伊勢市]]に鎮座する[[伊勢神宮]]内外両宮（[[皇大神宮|皇大神宮（内宮）]]と[[豊受大神宮|豊受大神宮（外宮）]]）が、現在地へ遷る以前に一時的にせよ祀られたという伝承を持つ神社・場所をいう。 伊勢内宮の[[祭神]]である[[天照大御神]]は[[皇祖神]]であるが、[[崇神天皇]]の時代までは[[天皇]]と「同床共殿」であったと伝えられ、つまり[[皇居|皇居内]]に祀られていたが、その状態を畏怖した同天皇が[[皇女]]である[[豊鍬入姫命|豊鋤入姫命]]にその神霊を託して[[倭国]][[笠縫邑]]に移したのに始まり、更に理想的な鎮座地を求めて各地を転々とし、[[垂仁天皇]]の第4皇女[[倭姫命]]がこれを引き継いで、およそ90年をかけて現在地に遷座したと伝わっている。その経緯は『[[古事記]]』にはこれを欠くものの、『[[日本書紀]]』に簡略に記され、『[[皇太神宮儀式帳]]』に更に詳しく、そして中世の『[[倭姫命世記]]』においてより詳述されている。また、外宮の祭神である[[豊受大御神]]は、「[[記紀]]」に記載を欠くものの、『[[止由気宮儀式帳]]』や『倭姫命世記』によれば[[雄略天皇]]の時代に天照大御神の[[神託]]によって[[丹波国]]（[[丹後国]]）から遷座したと伝えられている。 天照大御神が遍歴する説話は、『[[常陸国風土記]]』の[[筑波山]]の話に登場する祖神や民間説話の[[弘法大師]]伝説に類するもので、一般の[[神社]]の縁起でも鎮座地を求めて神が旅する話は多いので、「旅する神」の典型的な類型であるとされる。 ==元伊勢の一覧== ===皇大神宮=== *遷幸順に宮名（地名）と比定地（神社）または伝承地を記す。 *「日本紀」は『日本書紀』、「儀式帳」は『皇太神宮儀式帳』、「世記」は『倭姫命世記』における記載を表す。 *「世記」欄の括弧内は奉祭（滞在）年数である。 {| class="wikitable" !colspan=4 style="background-color:#C0C0C0; text-align:center"|[[豊鍬入姫命]]巡歴 |- |colspan=3|宮名（地名）||rowspan=2 style="width:47%"|比定地（伝承地） |- |style="width:15%"|日本紀||style="width:18%"|儀式帳||style="width:20%"|世記 |- |colspan=4 style="background-color:#C0C0C0;"|[[大和国|大和国（倭国）]] |- |rowspan=8|[[笠縫邑]]||rowspan=8| ||rowspan=8|笠縫邑（33年） |'''檜原神社'''（[[大神神社]]摂社）

'''元伊勢'''（もといせ）は、[[三重県]][[伊勢市]]に鎮座する[[伊勢神宮]]内外両宮（[[皇大神宮|皇大神宮（内宮）]]と[[豊受大神宮|豊受大神宮（外宮）]]）が、現在地へ遷る以前に一時的にせよ祀られたという伝承を持つ神社・場所をいう。 伊勢内宮の[[祭神]]である[[天照大御神]]は[[皇祖神]]であるが、[[崇神天皇]]の時代までは[[天皇]]と「同床共殿」であったと伝えられ、つまり[[皇居|皇居内]]に祀られていたが、その状態を畏怖した同天皇が[[皇女]]である[[豊鍬入姫命|豊鋤入姫命]]にその神霊を託して[[倭国]][[笠縫邑]]に移したのに始まり、更に理想的な鎮座地を求めて各地を転々とし、[[垂仁天皇]]の第4皇女[[倭姫命]]がこれを引き継いで、およそ90年をかけて現在地に遷座したと伝わっている。その経緯は『[[古事記]]』にはこれを欠くものの、『[[日本書紀]]』に簡略に記され、『[[皇太神宮儀式帳]]』に更に詳しく、そして中世の『[[倭姫命世記]]』においてより詳述されている。また、外宮の祭神である[[豊受大御神]]は、「[[記紀]]」に記載を欠くものの、『[[止由気宮儀式帳]]』や『倭姫命世記』によれば[[雄略天皇]]の時代に天照大御神の[[神託]]によって[[丹波国]]（[[丹後国]]）から遷座したと伝えられている。 天照大御神が遍歴する説話は、『[[常陸国風土記]]』の[[筑波山]]の話に登場する祖神や民間説話の[[弘法大師]]伝説に類するもので、一般の[[神社]]の縁起でも鎮座地を求めて神が旅する話は多いので、「旅する神」の典型的な類型であるとされる。 ==元伊勢の一覧== ===皇大神宮=== *遷幸順に宮名（地名）と比定地（神社）または伝承地を記す。 *「日本紀」は『日本書紀』、「儀式帳」は『皇太神宮儀式帳』、「世記」は『倭姫命世記』における記載を表す。 *「世記」欄の括弧内は奉祭（滞在）年数である。 {| class="wikitable" !colspan=4 style="background-color:#C0C0C0; text-align:center"|[[豊鍬入姫命]]巡歴 |- |colspan=3|宮名（地名）||rowspan=2 style="width:47%"|比定地（伝承地） |- |style="width:15%"|日本紀||style="width:18%"|儀式帳||style="width:20%"|世記 |- |colspan=4 style="background-color:#C0C0C0;"|[[大和国|大和国（倭国）]] |- |rowspan=8|[[笠縫邑]]||rowspan=8| ||rowspan=8|笠縫邑（33年） |'''檜原神社'''（[[大神神社]]摂社）

'''元伊勢'''（もといせ）は、[[三重県]][[伊勢市]]に鎮座する[[伊勢神宮]]内外両宮（[[皇大神宮|皇大神宮（内宮）]]と[[豊受大神宮|豊受大神宮（外宮）]]）が、現在地へ遷る以前に一時的にせよ祀られたという伝承を持つ神社・場所をいう。 伊勢内宮の[[祭神]]である[[天照大御神]]は[[皇祖神]]であるが、[[崇神天皇]]の時代までは[[天皇]]と「同床共殿」であったと伝えられ、つまり[[皇居|皇居内]]に祀られていたが、その状態を畏怖した同天皇が[[皇女]]である[[豊鍬入姫命|豊鋤入姫命]]にその神霊を託して[[倭国]][[笠縫邑]]に移したのに始まり、更に理想的な鎮座地を求めて各地を転々とし、[[垂仁天皇]]の第4皇女[[倭姫命]]がこれを引き継いで、およそ90年をかけて現在地に遷座したと伝わっている。その経緯は『[[古事記]]』にはこれを欠くものの、『[[日本書紀]]』で簡略に、『[[皇太神宮儀式帳]]』にやや詳しく、そして中世の『[[倭姫命世記]]』においてより詳述されている。また、外宮の祭神である[[豊受大御神]]は、「[[記紀]]」に記載を欠くものの、『[[止由気宮儀式帳]]』や『倭姫命世記』によれば[[雄略天皇]]の時代に天照大御神の[[神託]]によって[[丹波国]]（[[丹後国]]）から遷座したと伝えられている。 天照大御神が遍歴する説話は、『[[常陸国風土記]]』の[[筑波山]]の話に登場する祖神や民間説話の[[弘法大師]]伝説に類するもので、一般の[[神社]]の縁起でも鎮座地を求めて神が旅する話は多いので、「旅する神」の典型的な類型であるとされる。 ==元伊勢の一覧== ===皇大神宮=== *遷幸順に宮名（地名）と比定地（神社）または伝承地を記す。 *「日本紀」は『日本書紀』、「儀式帳」は『皇太神宮儀式帳』、「世記」は『倭姫命世記』における記載を表す。 *「世記」欄の括弧内は奉祭（滞在）年数である。 {| class="wikitable" !colspan=4 style="background-color:#C0C0C0; text-align:center"|[[豊鍬入姫命]]巡歴 |- |colspan=3|宮名（地名）||rowspan=2 style="width:47%"|比定地（伝承地） |- |style="width:15%"|日本紀||style="width:18%"|儀式帳||style="width:20%"|世記 |- |colspan=4 style="background-color:#C0C0C0;"|[[大和国|大和国（倭国）]] |- |rowspan=8|[[笠縫邑]]||rowspan=8| ||rowspan=8|笠縫邑（33年） |'''檜原神社'''（[[大神神社]]摂社）

'''元伊勢'''（もといせ）は、[[三重県]][[伊勢市]]に鎮座する[[伊勢神宮]]内外両宮（[[皇大神宮|皇大神宮（内宮）]]と[[豊受大神宮|豊受大神宮（外宮）]]）が、現在地へ遷る以前に一時的にせよ祀られたという伝承を持つ神社・場所をいう。 伊勢内宮の[[祭神]]である[[天照大御神]]は[[皇祖神]]であるが、[[崇神天皇]]の時代までは[[天皇]]と「同床共殿」であったと伝えられ、つまり[[皇居|皇居内]]に祀られていたが、その状態を畏怖した同天皇が[[皇女]]である[[豊鍬入姫命|豊鋤入姫命]]にその神霊を託して[[倭国]][[笠縫邑]]に移したのに始まり、更に理想的な鎮座地を求めて各地を転々とし、[[垂仁天皇]]の第4皇女[[倭姫命]]がこれを引き継いで、およそ90年をかけて現在地に遷座したと伝わっている。その経緯は『[[古事記]]』にはこれを欠くものの、『[[日本書紀]]』で簡略に、『[[皇太神宮儀式帳]]』にやや詳しく、そして中世の『[[倭姫命世記]]』においてより詳述されている。また、外宮の祭神である[[豊受大御神]]は、「[[記紀]]」に記載を欠くものの、『[[止由気宮儀式帳]]』や『倭姫命世記』によれば[[雄略天皇]]の時代に天照大御神の[[神託]]によって[[丹波国]]（[[丹後国]]）から遷座したと伝えられている。 天照大御神が遍歴する説話は、『[[常陸国風土記]]』の[[筑波山]]の話に登場する祖神や民間説話の[[弘法大師]]伝説に類するもので、一般の[[神社]]の縁起でも鎮座地を求めて神が旅する話は多いので、「旅する神」の典型的な類型であるとされる。 ==元伊勢の一覧== ===皇大神宮=== *遷幸順に宮名（地名）と比定地（神社）または伝承地を記す。 *「日本紀」は『日本書紀』、「儀式帳」は『皇太神宮儀式帳』、「世記」は『倭姫命世記』における記載を表す。 *「世記」欄の括弧内は奉祭（滞在）年数である。 {| class="wikitable" !colspan=4 style="background-color:#C0C0C0; text-align:center"|[[豊鍬入姫命]]巡歴 |- |colspan=3|宮名（地名）||rowspan=2 style="width:47%"|比定地（伝承地） |- |style="width:15%"|日本紀||style="width:18%"|儀式帳||style="width:20%"|世記 |- |colspan=4 style="background-color:#C0C0C0;"|[[大和国|大和国（倭国）]] |- |rowspan=8|[[笠縫邑]]||rowspan=8| ||rowspan=8|笠縫邑（33年） |'''檜原神社'''（[[大神神社]]摂社）

'''元伊勢'''（もといせ）は、[[三重県]][[伊勢市]]に鎮座する[[伊勢神宮]]内外両宮（[[皇大神宮|皇大神宮（内宮）]]と[[豊受大神宮|豊受大神宮（外宮）]]）が、現在地へ遷る以前に一時的にせよ祀られたという伝承を持つ神社・場所をいう。 伊勢内宮の[[祭神]]である[[天照大御神]]は[[皇祖神]]であるが、[[崇神天皇]]の時代までは[[天皇]]と「同床共殿」であったと伝えられ、つまり[[皇居|皇居内]]に祀られていたが、その状態を畏怖した同天皇が[[皇女]]である[[豊鍬入姫命|豊鋤入姫命]]にその神霊を託して[[倭国]][[笠縫邑]]に移したのに始まり、更に理想的な鎮座地を求めて各地を転々とし、[[垂仁天皇]]の第4皇女[[倭姫命]]がこれを引き継いで、およそ90年をかけて現在地に遷座したと伝わっている。その経緯は『[[古事記]]』にはこれを欠くものの、『[[日本書紀]]』で簡略に、『[[皇太神宮儀式帳]]』にやや詳しく、そして中世の『[[倭姫命世記]]』においてより詳述されている。また、外宮の祭神である[[豊受大御神]]は、「[[記紀]]」に記載を欠くものの、『[[止由気宮儀式帳]]』や『倭姫命世記』によれば[[雄略天皇]]の時代に天照大御神の[[神託]]によって[[丹波国]]（[[丹後国]]）から遷座したと伝えられている。 天照大御神が遍歴する説話は、『[[常陸国風土記]]』の[[筑波山]]の話に登場する祖神や民間説話の[[弘法大師]]伝説に類するもので、一般の[[神社]]の縁起でも鎮座地を求めて神が旅する話は多いので、「旅する神」の典型的な類型であるとされる。 ==元伊勢の一覧== ===皇大神宮=== *遷幸順に宮名（地名）と比定地（神社）または伝承地を記す。 *「日本紀」は『日本書紀』、「儀式帳」は『皇太神宮儀式帳』、「世記」は『倭姫命世記』における記載を表す。 *「世記」欄の括弧内は奉祭（滞在）年数である。 {| class="wikitable" !colspan=4 style="background-color:#C0C0C0; text-align:center"|[[豊鍬入姫命]]巡歴 |- |colspan=3|宮名（地名）||rowspan=2 style="width:47%"|比定地（伝承地） |- |style="width:15%"|日本紀||style="width:18%"|儀式帳||style="width:20%"|世記 |- |colspan=4 style="background-color:#C0C0C0;"|[[大和国|大和国（倭国）]] |- |rowspan=8|[[笠縫邑]]||rowspan=8| ||rowspan=8|笠縫邑（33年） |'''檜原神社'''（[[大神神社]]摂社）

'''元伊勢'''（もといせ）は、[[三重県]][[伊勢市]]に鎮座する[[伊勢神宮]]内外両宮（[[皇大神宮|皇大神宮（内宮）]]と[[豊受大神宮|豊受大神宮（外宮）]]）が、現在地へ遷る以前に一時的にせよ祀られたという伝承を持つ神社・場所をいう。 伊勢内宮の[[祭神]]である[[天照大御神]]は[[皇祖神]]であるが、[[崇神天皇]]の時代までは[[天皇]]と「同床共殿」であったと伝えられ、つまり[[皇居|皇居内]]に祀られていたが、その状態を畏怖した同天皇が[[皇女]]である[[豊鍬入姫命|豊鋤入姫命]]にその神霊を託して[[倭国]][[笠縫邑]]に移したのに始まり、更に理想的な鎮座地を求めて各地を転々とし、[[垂仁天皇]]の第4皇女[[倭姫命]]がこれを引き継いで、およそ90年をかけて現在地に遷座したと伝わっている。その経緯は『[[古事記]]』にはこれを欠くものの、『[[日本書紀]]』で簡略に、『[[皇太神宮儀式帳]]』にやや詳しく、そして中世の『[[倭姫命世記]]』においてより詳述されている。また、外宮の祭神である[[豊受大御神]]は、「[[記紀]]」に記載を欠くものの、『[[止由気宮儀式帳]]』や『倭姫命世記』によれば[[雄略天皇]]の時代に天照大御神の[[神託]]によって[[丹波国]]（[[丹後国]]）から遷座したと伝えられている。 天照大御神が遍歴する説話は、『[[常陸国風土記]]』の[[筑波山]]の話に登場する祖神や民間説話の[[弘法大師]]伝説に類するもので、一般の[[神社]]の縁起でも鎮座地を求めて神が旅する話は多いので、「旅する神」の典型的な類型であるとされる。 ==元伊勢の一覧== ===皇大神宮=== *遷幸順に宮名（地名）と比定地（神社）または伝承地を記す。 *「日本紀」は『日本書紀』、「儀式帳」は『皇太神宮儀式帳』、「世記」は『倭姫命世記』における記載を表す。 *「世記」欄の括弧内は奉祭（滞在）年数である。 {| class="wikitable" !colspan=4 style="background-color:#C0C0C0; text-align:center"|[[豊鍬入姫命]]巡歴 |- |colspan=3|宮名（地名）||rowspan=2 style="width:47%"|比定地（伝承地） |- |style="width:15%"|日本紀||style="width:18%"|儀式帳||style="width:20%"|世記 |- |colspan=4 style="background-color:#C0C0C0;"|[[大和国|大和国（倭国）]] |- |rowspan=8|[[笠縫邑]]||rowspan=8| ||rowspan=8|笠縫邑（33年） |'''檜原神社'''（[[大神神社]]摂社）

'''元伊勢'''（もといせ）は、[[三重県]][[伊勢市]]に鎮座する[[伊勢神宮]]内外両宮（[[皇大神宮|皇大神宮（内宮）]]と[[豊受大神宮|豊受大神宮（外宮）]]）が、現在地へ遷る以前に一時的にせよ祀られたという伝承を持つ神社・場所をいう。 伊勢内宮の[[祭神]]である[[天照大御神]]は[[皇祖神]]であるが、[[崇神天皇]]の時代までは[[天皇]]と「同床共殿」であったと伝えられ、つまり[[皇居|皇居内]]に祀られていたが、その状態を畏怖した同天皇が[[皇女]]である[[豊鍬入姫命|豊鋤入姫命]]にその神霊を託して[[倭国]][[笠縫邑]]に移したのに始まり、更に理想的な鎮座地を求めて各地を転々とし、[[垂仁天皇]]の第4皇女[[倭姫命]]がこれを引き継いで、およそ90年をかけて現在地に遷座したと伝わっている。その経緯は『[[古事記]]』にはこれを欠くものの、『[[日本書紀]]』で簡略に、『[[皇太神宮儀式帳]]』にやや詳しく、そして中世の『[[倭姫命世記]]』においてより詳述されている。また、外宮の祭神である[[豊受大御神]]は、「[[記紀]]」に記載を欠くものの、『[[止由気宮儀式帳]]』や『倭姫命世記』によれば[[雄略天皇]]の時代に天照大御神の[[神託]]によって[[丹波国]]（[[丹後国]]）から遷座したと伝えられている。 天照大御神が遍歴する説話は、『[[常陸国風土記]]』の[[筑波山]]の話に登場する祖神や民間説話の[[弘法大師]]伝説に類するもので、一般の[[神社]]の縁起でも鎮座地を求めて神が旅する話は多いので、「旅する神」の典型的な類型であるとされる。 ==元伊勢の一覧== ===皇大神宮=== *遷幸順に宮名（地名）と比定地（神社）または伝承地を記す。 *「日本紀」は『日本書紀』、「儀式帳」は『皇太神宮儀式帳』、「世記」は『倭姫命世記』における記載を表す。 *「世記」欄の括弧内は奉祭（滞在）年数である。 {| class="wikitable" !colspan=4 style="background-color:#C0C0C0; text-align:center"|[[豊鍬入姫命]]巡歴 |- |colspan=3|宮名（地名）||rowspan=2 style="width:47%"|比定地（伝承地） |- |style="width:15%"|日本紀||style="width:18%"|儀式帳||style="width:20%"|世記 |- |colspan=4 style="background-color:#C0C0C0;"|[[大和国|大和国（倭国）]] |- |rowspan=8|[[笠縫邑]]||rowspan=8| ||rowspan=8|笠縫邑（33年） |'''檜原神社'''（[[大神神社]]摂社）

Edward |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=7pEOicqsjv0C&dq=%22Moto-Ise%22&pg=PA201 |title=Himiko and Japan's Elusive Chiefdom of Yamatai: Archaeology, History, and Mythology |date=2007-02-28 |publisher=University of Hawaii Press |isbn=978-0-8248-3035-9 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Stalker |first=Nancy K. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=v44BEAAAQBAJ&dq=%22Moto-Ise%22&pg=PA62 |title=Prophet Motive: Deguchi Onisaburō, Oomoto, and the Rise of New Religions in Imperial Japan |date=2007-10-31 |publisher=University of Hawaii Press |isbn=978-0-8248-6404-0 |language=en}}</ref><ref name="iUniverse">{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=nPaezHFlfNQC&dq=%22Moto+Ise%22&pg=PT107|title=Where the Trees Grow Thick|publisher=iUniverse|isbn=978-0-595-28240-1|language=en}}</ref><ref name="Göttler-2017">{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=uyk_DwAAQBAJ&dq=%22Moto+Ise%22&pg=PA437|title=The Nomadic Object: The Challenge of World for Early Modern Religious Art|last1=Göttler|first1=Christine|last2=Mochizuki|first2=Mia|date=2017-11-06|publisher=BRILL|isbn=978-90-04-35450-0|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=PvgsAAAAIAAJ&dq=%22Moto+Ise%22&pg=RA3-PA147|title=Pamphlet - Dept. of the Army|last=Army|first=United States Department of the|date=1945|publisher=Headquarters, Department of the Army.|language=en}}</ref><ref name="Dougill-2023">{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=-H_cEAAAQBAJ&dq=%22Moto+Ise%22&pg=PT204|title=Off the Beaten Tracks in Japan: A Journey by Train from Hokkaido to Kyushu|last=Dougill|first=John|date=2023-11-07|publisher=Stone Bridge Press, Inc.|isbn=978-1-61172-963-4|language=en}}</ref> The first one was [[Ōmiwa Shrine|Hibara Shrine]] (a subshrine of [[Ōmiwa Shrine]]).<ref name="greenshinto">{{Cite web |last=D |first=John |date=2011-08-10 |title=Hibara Jinja and Amaterasu |url=https://www.greenshinto.com/2011/08/11/hibara-jinja-and-amaterasu/ |access-date=2023-10-18 |website=Green Shinto |language=en-GB}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Hibara Jinja Shrine（Nara） |url=https://www.jldb.bunka.go.jp/en/location/290100006/?search=1&q=Hibara+Shrine |access-date=2023-10-03 |website=Nationwide location database |language=en}}</ref><ref name="YAMATO UNKNOWN ORIGIN">{{Cite web |title=Omiwa Jinja Shrine/Sai Jinja Shrine/Kuehiko Jinja Shrine/Hibara Jinja Shrine│Destinations│Discover YAMATO│YAMATO UNKNOWN ORIGIN |url=http://www.city.sakurai.lg.jp/section/yamato-travel/destination/area01/spot02/ |access-date=2023-10-03 |website=YAMATO UNKNOWN ORIGIN |language=en}}</ref> Amaterasu was originally enshrined there before eventually moving to other Moto-Ise shrines and then finally to [[Ise Grand Shrine|Ise Jingu]].<ref name="YAMATO UNKNOWN ORIGIN" /><ref name="iUniverse" /><ref name="Göttler-2017" /><ref name="Dougill-2023" />
The journey was long so many shrines claim this title.<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=7pEOicqsjv0C&dq=%22Moto+Ise%22&pg=PA201|title=Himiko and Japan's Elusive Chiefdom of Yamatai: Archaeology, History, and Mythology|last=Kidder|first=J. Edward|date=2007-02-28|publisher=University of Hawaii Press|isbn=978-0-8248-3035-9|language=en}}</ref> These shrines are subject to a large amount of historical research.<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=XEIiEAAAQBAJ&dq=%22Moto+Ise%22&pg=PA534|title=RLE: Japan Mini-Set F: Philosophy and Religion (4 vols)|last=Authors|first=Various|date=2021-03-18|publisher=Routledge|isbn=978-1-136-90356-4|language=en}}</ref>
== Hibara Shrine == '''Hibara Shrine''' is a subshrine of Omiwa Shrine at the foot of {{ill|10=en|11=Mount_Miwa|12=fr|13=Mont Miwa|Mount Miwa|lt=Mount Miwa|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/10=en|qq=}} in [[Sakurai, Nara|Sakurai]], [[Nara Prefecture]]. The shrine is identified as the place where the {{ill|10=en|11=Yata-no-Kagami|Yata-no-Kagami|lt=Yata-no-Kagami|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/10=en|qq=}} and the {{ill|10=en|11=Kusanagi no Tsurugi|lt=Kusanagi-no-Tsurugi|Kusanagi no Tsurugi|lt=Kusanagi no Tsurugi|lt=Kusanagi-no-Tsurugi|lt=Kusanagi no Tsurugi|lt=Kusanagi-no-Tsurugi|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/10=en|qq=}} were first enshrined after they were removed from the imperial palace. It is the first of many {{ill|Moto-Ise Shrines|lt=Moto-Ise|ja|元伊勢|1=Moto-Ise Shrines|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Moto-Ise Shrines|13=User:Immanuelle/Moto-Ise Shrines|qq=}} shrines<ref name="greenshinto2">{{Cite web|last=D|first=John|date=2011-08-10|title=Hibara Jinja and Amaterasu|url=https://www.greenshinto.com/2011/08/11/hibara-jinja-and-amaterasu/|access-date=2023-10-18|website=Green Shinto|language=en-GB}}</ref>.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Hibara Jinja Shrine（Nara）|url=https://www.jldb.bunka.go.jp/en/location/290100006/?search=1&q=Hibara+Shrine|access-date=2023-10-03|website=Nationwide location database|language=en}}</ref><ref name="YAMATO UNKNOWN ORIGIN-2">{{Cite web|title=Omiwa Jinja Shrine/Sai Jinja Shrine/Kuehiko Jinja Shrine/Hibara Jinja Shrine│Destinations│Discover YAMATO│YAMATO UNKNOWN ORIGIN|url=http://www.city.sakurai.lg.jp/section/yamato-travel/destination/area01/spot02/|access-date=2023-10-03|website=YAMATO UNKNOWN ORIGIN|language=en}}</ref> Amaterasu was originally enshrined there before eventually moving to other Moto-Ise shrines and then finally to [[Ise Grand Shrine|Ise Jingu]].<ref name="YAMATO UNKNOWN ORIGIN-2" /> It has an [[Iwakura rock]] and a Shinza made of [[Sakaki]] wood.<ref name="YAMATO UNKNOWN ORIGIN-2" />
It has a prominent unique closable triple [[torii]] gate.<ref name="greenshinto2" />
== Summary == The deity enshrined at the Inner Shrine (内宮) of Ise Jingu (伊勢神宮), [[Amaterasu|Amaterasu Omikami]] (天照大御神), is considered the [[Oyagami|ancestral deity]] (皇祖神) of the emperors. Up until the era of the 10th Emperor, [[Emperor Sujin]] (崇神天皇), it is said that the emperor and Amaterasu Omikami shared the same residence, known as "sharing the same bed and palace" (同床共殿). Initially, she was enshrined within the [[Tokyo Imperial Palace|Imperial Palace]] (皇居), but fearing this arrangement, the emperor entrusted her divine spirit to Princess {{ill|Toyosukiiri-hime|ja|豊鍬入姫命|en:draft|simple|User:Immanuelle/Toyosukiiri-hime|fr|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Toyosukiiri-hime|qq=}} (豊鋤入姫命)<ref name="iUniverse" />, who established a sacred fence known as the "Iseki-no-himorogi" (磯城の神籬) in Iseshiro, Kasafu village (笠縫邑), [[Yamato Province|Yamato province]] (倭国). This began a search for an ideal location for her permanent enshrinement, which led to several relocations. Eventually, the 11th Emperor, [[Emperor Suinin|Emperor Suijin]]'s (垂仁天皇) fourth princess, Princess [[:en:Yamatohime-no-mikoto|Yamatohime-no-mikoto]] (倭姫命), took over this mission, and after approximately 90 years, the shrine was moved to its current location.<ref name="iUniverse" /><ref name="Dougill-2023" /> The "Iseki-no-himorogi" is first mentioned during the relocation of Amaterasu Omikami to Yamato Kasafu village in the Chronicles of Emperor Suinin, where it is imagined as a facility for the placement of a {{ill|Mirrors in Shinto|lt=Mirrors in Shinto|lt=Shinto mirror|lt=divine mirror|simple|User:Immanuelle/Shinto mirror|en|Mirrors in Shinto|fr|Miroirs dans le shintoïsme|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinto mirror|qq=}}, symbolizing a sacred area akin to a rock seat, with a vast horizontal landscape preserving the tradition of the Iseshiro form. At Ise Jingu, the Shin-no-mihashira (心御柱), a central sacred pillar, is largely buried in the ground with its surroundings wrapped in sakaki (榊), and ritual pottery symbolizes the rituals. It is said that when the divine mirror of Amaterasu Omikami was first dedicated, a five-hundred-year-old tree from {{ill|Mount Amanokagu|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mount Amanokagu|qq=}} was dug up, with jewels hung on its upper branches and a mirror on its middle branches, but the sakaki-decorated Shin-no-mihashira symbolizes the appearance of this sacred tree during rituals. The relocation process is not mentioned in the "[[Kojiki]]," but is briefly noted in the "[[Nihon Shoki]]," more detailed in the "{{ill|Kotai Jingu Gishiki|ja|皇太神宮儀式帳|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kotai Jingu Gishiki|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 延暦儀式帳}}," and most elaborately in the "{{ill|Yamatohime-no-mikoto Seiki|ja|倭姫命世記|1=Yamatohime no Mikoto Seiki|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yamatohime-no-mikoto Seiki|13=User:Immanuelle/Yamatohime no Mikoto Seiki|qq=}}," a medieval text from the "{{ill|Shintō Gobusho|lt=Shintō Gobusho|lt=Shinto Gobusho|ja|神道五部書|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinto Gobusho|qq=}} (神道五部書)."
The deity of the Outer Shrine (外宮), [[Toyouke-hime|Toyouke-no-Ōmikami]] (豊受大御神), although not mentioned in the "[[Kojiki]]" or "[[Nihon Shoki]]," is said in the "{{ill|Toyuke Gū Gishiki|ja|止由気宮儀式帳|lt=Toyuke Shrine Ritual Book|lt_ja=止由気宮儀式帳|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Toyuke Gū Gishiki|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 延暦儀式帳}}" and "{{ill|Yamatohime-no-mikoto Seiki|ja|倭姫命世記|lt=Yamatohime-no-mikoto Chronicles|lt_ja=倭姫命世記|1=Yamatohime no Mikoto Seiki|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yamatohime-no-mikoto Seiki|13=User:Immanuelle/Yamatohime no Mikoto Seiki|qq=}}" to have been relocated from Tango Province (丹後国) (now part of Tanba Province (丹波国)) to her current site by divine command of Amaterasu Omikami during the era of the 21st Emperor, Emperor Yūryaku (雄略天皇).
The tale of Amaterasu Omikami's wanderings is considered similar to the ancestral deity stories in the "{{ill|Hitachi Province Fudoki|ja|常陸国風土記|zh|常陸國風土記|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hitachi Province Fudoki|qq=}}" about {{ill|Mount Tsukuba|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mount Tsukuba|qq=}} (筑波山) and the folk tales about {{ill|Kūkai|4=en|6=fr|8=ja|9=弘法大師|10=simple|11=User:Immanuelle/Kūkai|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kūkai|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 空海}} (弘法大師). Since many shrine origin stories involve deities traveling to find their enshrinement locations, this is considered a typical motif of a "traveling deity."
The origin tradition of the "Former Ise" is derived from texts like the "{{ill|Kotai Jingu Gishiki|ja|皇太神宮儀式帳|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kotai Jingu Gishiki|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 延暦儀式帳}}, {{ill|Toyuke Gū Gishiki|ja|止由気宮儀式帳|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Toyuke Gū Gishiki|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 延暦儀式帳}}, {{ill|Kogo Shūi|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kogo Shūi|qq=}}, and [[Engishiki]]." Although it was previously said to involve around twenty locations, it now includes over sixty. These traditions are based on those transmitted to various shrines, and there are cases where nearby locations claim to be the traditional site, leaving the truth of these claims unclear.
==Oomoto== A Moto-Ise Shrine "North of {{ill|Ayabe, Kyoto|lt=Ayabe|en|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ayabe, Kyoto|qq=}}", {{ill|Amanoiwato Shrine|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Amanoiwato Shrine|qq=}} was used in a symbolic act by the religious group Oomoto to emphasize their spiritual authority and connection to Japan's ancient religious traditions. Specifically, members of Oomoto collected sacred elements—fire, water, and earth—from [[Izumo-taisha]] during a pilgrimage. They then combined these elements with water from Moto-Ise, a site revered as the original location of the Ise Shrine and associated with the goddess Amaterasu. By mixing these sacred substances, Oomoto was asserting a deep and direct link to the ancient and most sacred sites of Shinto, effectively positioning themselves as a leading advocate for Japan's traditional spiritual practices.<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=v44BEAAAQBAJ&dq=%22Moto+Ise%22&pg=PA62|title=Prophet Motive: Deguchi Onisaburō, Oomoto, and the Rise of New Religions in Imperial Japan|last=Stalker|first=Nancy K.|date=2007-10-31|publisher=University of Hawaii Press|isbn=978-0-8248-6404-0|language=en|qq=draft}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Nao Deguchi A Biography of the Foundress of Oomoto|url=https://www.oomoto.or.jp/English/enKyos/kaisoden/index.html|access-date=2024-05-05|website=www.oomoto.or.jp}}</ref> Their headquarters are near this "Moto-Ise"<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=xlG3F6gSm9UC&dq=%22Moto+Ise%22&pg=PA232|title=Historical Dictionary of Shinto|last=Picken|first=Stuart D. B.|date=2010-12-28|publisher=Scarecrow Press|isbn=978-0-8108-7372-8|language=en}}</ref>.

Edward |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=7pEOicqsjv0C&dq=%22Moto-Ise%22&pg=PA201 |title=Himiko and Japan's Elusive Chiefdom of Yamatai: Archaeology, History, and Mythology |date=2007-02-28 |publisher=University of Hawaii Press |isbn=978-0-8248-3035-9 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Stalker |first=Nancy K. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=v44BEAAAQBAJ&dq=%22Moto-Ise%22&pg=PA62 |title=Prophet Motive: Deguchi Onisaburō, Oomoto, and the Rise of New Religions in Imperial Japan |date=2007-10-31 |publisher=University of Hawaii Press |isbn=978-0-8248-6404-0 |language=en}}</ref><ref name="iUniverse">{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=nPaezHFlfNQC&dq=%22Moto+Ise%22&pg=PT107|title=Where the Trees Grow Thick|publisher=iUniverse|isbn=978-0-595-28240-1|language=en}}</ref><ref name="Göttler-2017">{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=uyk_DwAAQBAJ&dq=%22Moto+Ise%22&pg=PA437|title=The Nomadic Object: The Challenge of World for Early Modern Religious Art|last1=Göttler|first1=Christine|last2=Mochizuki|first2=Mia|date=2017-11-06|publisher=BRILL|isbn=978-90-04-35450-0|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=PvgsAAAAIAAJ&dq=%22Moto+Ise%22&pg=RA3-PA147|title=Pamphlet - Dept. of the Army|last=Army|first=United States Department of the|date=1945|publisher=Headquarters, Department of the Army.|language=en}}</ref><ref name="Dougill-2023">{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=-H_cEAAAQBAJ&dq=%22Moto+Ise%22&pg=PT204|title=Off the Beaten Tracks in Japan: A Journey by Train from Hokkaido to Kyushu|last=Dougill|first=John|date=2023-11-07|publisher=Stone Bridge Press, Inc.|isbn=978-1-61172-963-4|language=en}}</ref> The first one was [[:en:Ōmiwa Shrine|Hibara Shrine]] (a subshrine of [[:en:Ōmiwa Shrine|Ōmiwa Shrine]]).<ref name="greenshinto">{{Cite web |last=D |first=John |date=2011-08-10 |title=Hibara Jinja and Amaterasu |url=https://www.greenshinto.com/2011/08/11/hibara-jinja-and-amaterasu/ |access-date=2023-10-18 |website=Green Shinto |language=en-GB}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Hibara Jinja Shrine（Nara） |url=https://www.jldb.bunka.go.jp/en/location/290100006/?search=1&q=Hibara+Shrine |access-date=2023-10-03 |website=Nationwide location database |language=en}}</ref><ref name="YAMATO UNKNOWN ORIGIN">{{Cite web |title=Omiwa Jinja Shrine/Sai Jinja Shrine/Kuehiko Jinja Shrine/Hibara Jinja Shrine│Destinations│Discover YAMATO│YAMATO UNKNOWN ORIGIN |url=http://www.city.sakurai.lg.jp/section/yamato-travel/destination/area01/spot02/ |access-date=2023-10-03 |website=YAMATO UNKNOWN ORIGIN |language=en}}</ref> Amaterasu was originally enshrined there before eventually moving to other Moto-Ise shrines and then finally to [[Ise Grand Shrine|Ise Jingu]].<ref name="YAMATO UNKNOWN ORIGIN" /><ref name="iUniverse" /><ref name="Göttler-2017" /><ref name="Dougill-2023" />
The journey was long so many shrines claim this title.<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=7pEOicqsjv0C&dq=%22Moto+Ise%22&pg=PA201|title=Himiko and Japan's Elusive Chiefdom of Yamatai: Archaeology, History, and Mythology|last=Kidder|first=J. Edward|date=2007-02-28|publisher=University of Hawaii Press|isbn=978-0-8248-3035-9|language=en}}</ref> These shrines are subject to a large amount of historical research.<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=XEIiEAAAQBAJ&dq=%22Moto+Ise%22&pg=PA534|title=RLE: Japan Mini-Set F: Philosophy and Religion (4 vols)|last=Authors|first=Various|date=2021-03-18|publisher=Routledge|isbn=978-1-136-90356-4|language=en}}</ref>
== Hibara Shrine == '''Hibara Shrine''' is a subshrine of Omiwa Shrine at the foot of {{ill|10=en|11=Mount_Miwa|12=fr|13=Mont Miwa|Mount Miwa|lt=Mount Miwa|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/10=en|qq=}} in [[Sakurai, Nara|Sakurai]], [[Nara Prefecture]]. The shrine is identified as the place where the {{ill|10=en|11=Yata-no-Kagami|Yata-no-Kagami|lt=Yata-no-Kagami|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/10=en|qq=}} and the {{ill|10=en|11=Kusanagi no Tsurugi|lt=Kusanagi-no-Tsurugi|Kusanagi no Tsurugi|lt=Kusanagi no Tsurugi|lt=Kusanagi-no-Tsurugi|lt=Kusanagi no Tsurugi|lt=Kusanagi-no-Tsurugi|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/10=en|qq=}} were first enshrined after they were removed from the imperial palace. It is the first of many {{ill|Moto-Ise Shrines|lt=Moto-Ise|ja|元伊勢|1=Moto-Ise Shrines|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Moto-Ise Shrines|13=User:Immanuelle/Moto-Ise Shrines|qq=}} shrines<ref name="greenshinto2">{{Cite web|last=D|first=John|date=2011-08-10|title=Hibara Jinja and Amaterasu|url=https://www.greenshinto.com/2011/08/11/hibara-jinja-and-amaterasu/|access-date=2023-10-18|website=Green Shinto|language=en-GB}}</ref>.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Hibara Jinja Shrine（Nara）|url=https://www.jldb.bunka.go.jp/en/location/290100006/?search=1&q=Hibara+Shrine|access-date=2023-10-03|website=Nationwide location database|language=en}}</ref><ref name="YAMATO UNKNOWN ORIGIN-2">{{Cite web|title=Omiwa Jinja Shrine/Sai Jinja Shrine/Kuehiko Jinja Shrine/Hibara Jinja Shrine│Destinations│Discover YAMATO│YAMATO UNKNOWN ORIGIN|url=http://www.city.sakurai.lg.jp/section/yamato-travel/destination/area01/spot02/|access-date=2023-10-03|website=YAMATO UNKNOWN ORIGIN|language=en}}</ref> Amaterasu was originally enshrined there before eventually moving to other Moto-Ise shrines and then finally to [[Ise Grand Shrine|Ise Jingu]].<ref name="YAMATO UNKNOWN ORIGIN-2" /> It has an [[Iwakura rock]] and a Shinza made of [[Sakaki]] wood.<ref name="YAMATO UNKNOWN ORIGIN-2" />
It has a prominent unique closable triple [[torii]] gate.<ref name="greenshinto2" />
== Summary == The deity enshrined at the Inner Shrine (内宮) of Ise Jingu (伊勢神宮), [[Amaterasu|Amaterasu Omikami]] (天照大御神), is considered the [[Oyagami|ancestral deity]] (皇祖神) of the emperors. Up until the era of the 10th Emperor, [[Emperor Sujin]] (崇神天皇), it is said that the emperor and Amaterasu Omikami shared the same residence, known as "sharing the same bed and palace" (同床共殿). Initially, she was enshrined within the [[Tokyo Imperial Palace|Imperial Palace]] (皇居), but fearing this arrangement, the emperor entrusted her divine spirit to Princess {{ill|Toyosukiiri-hime|ja|豊鍬入姫命|en:draft|simple|User:Immanuelle/Toyosukiiri-hime|fr|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Toyosukiiri-hime|qq=}} (豊鋤入姫命)<ref name="iUniverse" />, who established a sacred fence known as the "Iseki-no-himorogi" (磯城の神籬) in Iseshiro, Kasafu village (笠縫邑), [[Yamato Province|Yamato province]] (倭国). This began a search for an ideal location for her permanent enshrinement, which led to several relocations. Eventually, the 11th Emperor, [[Emperor Suinin|Emperor Suijin]]'s (垂仁天皇) fourth princess, Princess [[:en:Yamatohime-no-mikoto|Yamatohime-no-mikoto]] (倭姫命), took over this mission, and after approximately 90 years, the shrine was moved to its current location.<ref name="iUniverse" /><ref name="Dougill-2023" /> The "Iseki-no-himorogi" is first mentioned during the relocation of Amaterasu Omikami to Yamato Kasafu village in the Chronicles of Emperor Suinin, where it is imagined as a facility for the placement of a {{ill|Mirrors in Shinto|lt=Mirrors in Shinto|lt=Shinto mirror|lt=divine mirror|simple|User:Immanuelle/Shinto mirror|en|Mirrors in Shinto|fr|Miroirs dans le shintoïsme|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinto mirror|qq=}}, symbolizing a sacred area akin to a rock seat, with a vast horizontal landscape preserving the tradition of the Iseshiro form. At Ise Jingu, the Shin-no-mihashira (心御柱), a central sacred pillar, is largely buried in the ground with its surroundings wrapped in sakaki (榊), and ritual pottery symbolizes the rituals. It is said that when the divine mirror of Amaterasu Omikami was first dedicated, a five-hundred-year-old tree from {{ill|Mount Amanokagu|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mount Amanokagu|qq=}} was dug up, with jewels hung on its upper branches and a mirror on its middle branches, but the sakaki-decorated Shin-no-mihashira symbolizes the appearance of this sacred tree during rituals. The relocation process is not mentioned in the "[[Kojiki]]," but is briefly noted in the "[[Nihon Shoki]]," more detailed in the "{{ill|Kotai Jingu Gishiki|ja|皇太神宮儀式帳|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kotai Jingu Gishiki|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 延暦儀式帳}}," and most elaborately in the "{{ill|Yamatohime-no-mikoto Seiki|ja|倭姫命世記|1=Yamatohime no Mikoto Seiki|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yamatohime-no-mikoto Seiki|13=User:Immanuelle/Yamatohime no Mikoto Seiki|qq=}}," a medieval text from the "{{ill|Shintō Gobusho|lt=Shintō Gobusho|lt=Shinto Gobusho|ja|神道五部書|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinto Gobusho|qq=}} (神道五部書)."
The deity of the Outer Shrine (外宮), [[Toyouke-hime|Toyouke-no-Ōmikami]] (豊受大御神), although not mentioned in the "[[Kojiki]]" or "[[Nihon Shoki]]," is said in the "{{ill|Toyuke Gū Gishiki|ja|止由気宮儀式帳|lt=Toyuke Shrine Ritual Book|lt_ja=止由気宮儀式帳|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Toyuke Gū Gishiki|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 延暦儀式帳}}" and "{{ill|Yamatohime-no-mikoto Seiki|ja|倭姫命世記|lt=Yamatohime-no-mikoto Chronicles|lt_ja=倭姫命世記|1=Yamatohime no Mikoto Seiki|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yamatohime-no-mikoto Seiki|13=User:Immanuelle/Yamatohime no Mikoto Seiki|qq=}}" to have been relocated from Tango Province (丹後国) (now part of Tanba Province (丹波国)) to her current site by divine command of Amaterasu Omikami during the era of the 21st Emperor, Emperor Yūryaku (雄略天皇).
The tale of Amaterasu Omikami's wanderings is considered similar to the ancestral deity stories in the "{{ill|Hitachi Province Fudoki|ja|常陸国風土記|zh|常陸國風土記|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hitachi Province Fudoki|qq=}}" about {{ill|Mount Tsukuba|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mount Tsukuba|qq=}} (筑波山) and the folk tales about {{ill|Kūkai|4=en|6=fr|8=ja|9=弘法大師|10=simple|11=User:Immanuelle/Kūkai|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kūkai|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 空海}} (弘法大師). Since many shrine origin stories involve deities traveling to find their enshrinement locations, this is considered a typical motif of a "traveling deity."
The origin tradition of the "Former Ise" is derived from texts like the "{{ill|Kotai Jingu Gishiki|ja|皇太神宮儀式帳|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kotai Jingu Gishiki|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 延暦儀式帳}}, {{ill|Toyuke Gū Gishiki|ja|止由気宮儀式帳|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Toyuke Gū Gishiki|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 延暦儀式帳}}, {{ill|Kogo Shūi|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kogo Shūi|qq=}}, and [[Engishiki]]." Although it was previously said to involve around twenty locations, it now includes over sixty. These traditions are based on those transmitted to various shrines, and there are cases where nearby locations claim to be the traditional site, leaving the truth of these claims unclear.
==Oomoto== A Moto-Ise Shrine "North of {{ill|Ayabe, Kyoto|lt=Ayabe|en|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ayabe, Kyoto|qq=}}", {{ill|Amanoiwato Shrine|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Amanoiwato Shrine|qq=}} was used in a symbolic act by the religious group Oomoto to emphasize their spiritual authority and connection to Japan's ancient religious traditions. Specifically, members of Oomoto collected sacred elements—fire, water, and earth—from [[Izumo-taisha]] during a pilgrimage. They then combined these elements with water from Moto-Ise, a site revered as the original location of the Ise Shrine and associated with the goddess Amaterasu. By mixing these sacred substances, Oomoto was asserting a deep and direct link to the ancient and most sacred sites of Shinto, effectively positioning themselves as a leading advocate for Japan's traditional spiritual practices.<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=v44BEAAAQBAJ&dq=%22Moto+Ise%22&pg=PA62|title=Prophet Motive: Deguchi Onisaburō, Oomoto, and the Rise of New Religions in Imperial Japan|last=Stalker|first=Nancy K.|date=2007-10-31|publisher=University of Hawaii Press|isbn=978-0-8248-6404-0|language=en|qq=draft}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Nao Deguchi A Biography of the Foundress of Oomoto|url=https://www.oomoto.or.jp/English/enKyos/kaisoden/index.html|access-date=2024-05-05|website=www.oomoto.or.jp}}</ref> Their headquarters are near this "Moto-Ise"<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=xlG3F6gSm9UC&dq=%22Moto+Ise%22&pg=PA232|title=Historical Dictionary of Shinto|last=Picken|first=Stuart D. B.|date=2010-12-28|publisher=Scarecrow Press|isbn=978-0-8108-7372-8|language=en}}</ref>.

[[File:Hibara-jinja,_torii_closeup.jpg|link=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Hibara-jinja,_torii_closeup.jpg|thumb|Miwa Torii demonstrating both their threefold nature and the closed gate]] {{ill|Moto-Ise Shrines|ja|元伊勢|1=Moto-Ise Shrines|fr|Sanctuaires Moto-Ise|en:draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Moto-Ise Shrines|13=User:Immanuelle/Moto-Ise Shrines|qq=}} are [[Shinto shrines]] that used to host Amaterasu before she was moved to [[Ise Grand Shrine|Ise Jingu]].<ref>{{Cite book |last=Kidder |first=J. Edward |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=7pEOicqsjv0C&dq=%22Moto-Ise%22&pg=PA201 |title=Himiko and Japan's Elusive Chiefdom of Yamatai: Archaeology, History, and Mythology |date=2007-02-28 |publisher=University of Hawaii Press |isbn=978-0-8248-3035-9 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Stalker |first=Nancy K. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=v44BEAAAQBAJ&dq=%22Moto-Ise%22&pg=PA62 |title=Prophet Motive: Deguchi Onisaburō, Oomoto, and the Rise of New Religions in Imperial Japan |date=2007-10-31 |publisher=University of Hawaii Press |isbn=978-0-8248-6404-0 |language=en}}</ref><ref name="iUniverse">{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=nPaezHFlfNQC&dq=%22Moto+Ise%22&pg=PT107|title=Where the Trees Grow Thick|publisher=iUniverse|isbn=978-0-595-28240-1|language=en}}</ref><ref name="Göttler-2017">{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=uyk_DwAAQBAJ&dq=%22Moto+Ise%22&pg=PA437|title=The Nomadic Object: The Challenge of World for Early Modern Religious Art|last1=Göttler|first1=Christine|last2=Mochizuki|first2=Mia|date=2017-11-06|publisher=BRILL|isbn=978-90-04-35450-0|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=PvgsAAAAIAAJ&dq=%22Moto+Ise%22&pg=RA3-PA147|title=Pamphlet - Dept. of the Army|last=Army|first=United States Department of the|date=1945|publisher=Headquarters, Department of the Army.|language=en}}</ref><ref name="Dougill-2023">{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=-H_cEAAAQBAJ&dq=%22Moto+Ise%22&pg=PT204|title=Off the Beaten Tracks in Japan: A Journey by Train from Hokkaido to Kyushu|last=Dougill|first=John|date=2023-11-07|publisher=Stone Bridge Press, Inc.|isbn=978-1-61172-963-4|language=en}}</ref> The first one was [[:en:Ōmiwa Shrine|Hibara Shrine]] (a subshrine of [[:en:Ōmiwa Shrine|Ōmiwa Shrine]]).<ref name="greenshinto">{{Cite web |last=D |first=John |date=2011-08-10 |title=Hibara Jinja and Amaterasu |url=https://www.greenshinto.com/2011/08/11/hibara-jinja-and-amaterasu/ |access-date=2023-10-18 |website=Green Shinto |language=en-GB}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Hibara Jinja Shrine（Nara） |url=https://www.jldb.bunka.go.jp/en/location/290100006/?search=1&q=Hibara+Shrine |access-date=2023-10-03 |website=Nationwide location database |language=en}}</ref><ref name="YAMATO UNKNOWN ORIGIN">{{Cite web |title=Omiwa Jinja Shrine/Sai Jinja Shrine/Kuehiko Jinja Shrine/Hibara Jinja Shrine│Destinations│Discover YAMATO│YAMATO UNKNOWN ORIGIN |url=http://www.city.sakurai.lg.jp/section/yamato-travel/destination/area01/spot02/ |access-date=2023-10-03 |website=YAMATO UNKNOWN ORIGIN |language=en}}</ref> Amaterasu was originally enshrined there before eventually moving to other Moto-Ise shrines and then finally to [[Ise Grand Shrine|Ise Jingu]].<ref name="YAMATO UNKNOWN ORIGIN" /><ref name="iUniverse" /><ref name="Göttler-2017" /><ref name="Dougill-2023" />
The journey was long so many shrines claim this title.<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=7pEOicqsjv0C&dq=%22Moto+Ise%22&pg=PA201|title=Himiko and Japan's Elusive Chiefdom of Yamatai: Archaeology, History, and Mythology|last=Kidder|first=J. Edward|date=2007-02-28|publisher=University of Hawaii Press|isbn=978-0-8248-3035-9|language=en}}</ref> These shrines are subject to a large amount of historical research.<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=XEIiEAAAQBAJ&dq=%22Moto+Ise%22&pg=PA534|title=RLE: Japan Mini-Set F: Philosophy and Religion (4 vols)|last=Authors|first=Various|date=2021-03-18|publisher=Routledge|isbn=978-1-136-90356-4|language=en}}</ref>
== Hibara Shrine == '''Hibara Shrine''' is a subshrine of Omiwa Shrine at the foot of {{ill|10=en|11=Mount_Miwa|12=fr|13=Mont Miwa|Mount Miwa|lt=Mount Miwa|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/10=en|qq=}} in [[Sakurai, Nara|Sakurai]], [[Nara Prefecture]]. The shrine is identified as the place where the {{ill|10=en|11=Yata-no-Kagami|Yata-no-Kagami|lt=Yata-no-Kagami|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/10=en|qq=}} and the {{ill|10=en|11=Kusanagi no Tsurugi|lt=Kusanagi-no-Tsurugi|Kusanagi no Tsurugi|lt=Kusanagi no Tsurugi|lt=Kusanagi-no-Tsurugi|lt=Kusanagi no Tsurugi|lt=Kusanagi-no-Tsurugi|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/10=en|qq=}} were first enshrined after they were removed from the imperial palace. It is the first of many {{ill|Moto-Ise Shrines|lt=Moto-Ise|ja|元伊勢|1=Moto-Ise Shrines|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Moto-Ise Shrines|13=User:Immanuelle/Moto-Ise Shrines|qq=}} shrines<ref name="greenshinto2">{{Cite web|last=D|first=John|date=2011-08-10|title=Hibara Jinja and Amaterasu|url=https://www.greenshinto.com/2011/08/11/hibara-jinja-and-amaterasu/|access-date=2023-10-18|website=Green Shinto|language=en-GB}}</ref>.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Hibara Jinja Shrine（Nara）|url=https://www.jldb.bunka.go.jp/en/location/290100006/?search=1&q=Hibara+Shrine|access-date=2023-10-03|website=Nationwide location database|language=en}}</ref><ref name="YAMATO UNKNOWN ORIGIN-2">{{Cite web|title=Omiwa Jinja Shrine/Sai Jinja Shrine/Kuehiko Jinja Shrine/Hibara Jinja Shrine│Destinations│Discover YAMATO│YAMATO UNKNOWN ORIGIN|url=http://www.city.sakurai.lg.jp/section/yamato-travel/destination/area01/spot02/|access-date=2023-10-03|website=YAMATO UNKNOWN ORIGIN|language=en}}</ref> Amaterasu was originally enshrined there before eventually moving to other Moto-Ise shrines and then finally to [[Ise Grand Shrine|Ise Jingu]].<ref name="YAMATO UNKNOWN ORIGIN-2" /> It has an [[Iwakura rock]] and a Shinza made of [[Sakaki]] wood.<ref name="YAMATO UNKNOWN ORIGIN-2" />
It has a prominent unique closable triple [[torii]] gate.<ref name="greenshinto2" />
== Summary == The deity enshrined at the Inner Shrine (内宮) of Ise Jingu (伊勢神宮), [[Amaterasu|Amaterasu Omikami]] (天照大御神), is considered the [[Oyagami|ancestral deity]] (皇祖神) of the emperors. Up until the era of the 10th Emperor, [[Emperor Sujin]] (崇神天皇), it is said that the emperor and Amaterasu Omikami shared the same residence, known as "sharing the same bed and palace" (同床共殿). Initially, she was enshrined within the [[Tokyo Imperial Palace|Imperial Palace]] (皇居), but fearing this arrangement, the emperor entrusted her divine spirit to Princess {{ill|Toyosukiiri-hime|ja|豊鍬入姫命|en:draft|simple|User:Immanuelle/Toyosukiiri-hime|fr|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Toyosukiiri-hime|qq=}} (豊鋤入姫命)<ref name="iUniverse" />, who established a sacred fence known as the "Iseki-no-himorogi" (磯城の神籬) in Iseshiro, Kasafu village (笠縫邑), [[Yamato Province|Yamato province]] (倭国). This began a search for an ideal location for her permanent enshrinement, which led to several relocations. Eventually, the 11th Emperor, [[:en:Emperor Suinin|Emperor Suijin]]'s (垂仁天皇) fourth princess, Princess [[:en:Yamatohime-no-mikoto|Yamatohime-no-mikoto]] (倭姫命), took over this mission, and after approximately 90 years, the shrine was moved to its current location.<ref name="iUniverse" /><ref name="Dougill-2023" /> The "Iseki-no-himorogi" is first mentioned during the relocation of Amaterasu Omikami to Yamato Kasafu village in the Chronicles of Emperor Suinin, where it is imagined as a facility for the placement of a {{ill|Mirrors in Shinto|lt=Mirrors in Shinto|lt=Shinto mirror|lt=divine mirror|simple|User:Immanuelle/Shinto mirror|en|Mirrors in Shinto|fr|Miroirs dans le shintoïsme|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinto mirror|qq=}}, symbolizing a sacred area akin to a rock seat, with a vast horizontal landscape preserving the tradition of the Iseshiro form. At Ise Jingu, the Shin-no-mihashira (心御柱), a central sacred pillar, is largely buried in the ground with its surroundings wrapped in sakaki (榊), and ritual pottery symbolizes the rituals. It is said that when the divine mirror of Amaterasu Omikami was first dedicated, a five-hundred-year-old tree from {{ill|Mount Amanokagu|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mount Amanokagu|qq=}} was dug up, with jewels hung on its upper branches and a mirror on its middle branches, but the sakaki-decorated Shin-no-mihashira symbolizes the appearance of this sacred tree during rituals. The relocation process is not mentioned in the "[[Kojiki]]," but is briefly noted in the "[[Nihon Shoki]]," more detailed in the "{{ill|Kotai Jingu Gishiki|ja|皇太神宮儀式帳|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kotai Jingu Gishiki|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 延暦儀式帳}}," and most elaborately in the "{{ill|Yamatohime-no-mikoto Seiki|ja|倭姫命世記|1=Yamatohime no Mikoto Seiki|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yamatohime-no-mikoto Seiki|13=User:Immanuelle/Yamatohime no Mikoto Seiki|qq=}}," a medieval text from the "{{ill|Shintō Gobusho|lt=Shintō Gobusho|lt=Shinto Gobusho|ja|神道五部書|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinto Gobusho|qq=}} (神道五部書)."
The deity of the Outer Shrine (外宮), [[Toyouke-hime|Toyouke-no-Ōmikami]] (豊受大御神), although not mentioned in the "[[Kojiki]]" or "[[Nihon Shoki]]," is said in the "{{ill|Toyuke Gū Gishiki|ja|止由気宮儀式帳|lt=Toyuke Shrine Ritual Book|lt_ja=止由気宮儀式帳|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Toyuke Gū Gishiki|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 延暦儀式帳}}" and "{{ill|Yamatohime-no-mikoto Seiki|ja|倭姫命世記|lt=Yamatohime-no-mikoto Chronicles|lt_ja=倭姫命世記|1=Yamatohime no Mikoto Seiki|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yamatohime-no-mikoto Seiki|13=User:Immanuelle/Yamatohime no Mikoto Seiki|qq=}}" to have been relocated from Tango Province (丹後国) (now part of Tanba Province (丹波国)) to her current site by divine command of Amaterasu Omikami during the era of the 21st Emperor, Emperor Yūryaku (雄略天皇).
The tale of Amaterasu Omikami's wanderings is considered similar to the ancestral deity stories in the "{{ill|Hitachi Province Fudoki|ja|常陸国風土記|zh|常陸國風土記|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hitachi Province Fudoki|qq=}}" about {{ill|Mount Tsukuba|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mount Tsukuba|qq=}} (筑波山) and the folk tales about {{ill|Kūkai|4=en|6=fr|8=ja|9=弘法大師|10=simple|11=User:Immanuelle/Kūkai|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kūkai|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 空海}} (弘法大師). Since many shrine origin stories involve deities traveling to find their enshrinement locations, this is considered a typical motif of a "traveling deity."
The origin tradition of the "Former Ise" is derived from texts like the "{{ill|Kotai Jingu Gishiki|ja|皇太神宮儀式帳|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kotai Jingu Gishiki|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 延暦儀式帳}}, {{ill|Toyuke Gū Gishiki|ja|止由気宮儀式帳|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Toyuke Gū Gishiki|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 延暦儀式帳}}, {{ill|Kogo Shūi|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kogo Shūi|qq=}}, and [[Engishiki]]." Although it was previously said to involve around twenty locations, it now includes over sixty. These traditions are based on those transmitted to various shrines, and there are cases where nearby locations claim to be the traditional site, leaving the truth of these claims unclear.
==Oomoto== A Moto-Ise Shrine "North of {{ill|Ayabe, Kyoto|lt=Ayabe|en|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ayabe, Kyoto|qq=}}", {{ill|Amanoiwato Shrine|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Amanoiwato Shrine|qq=}} was used in a symbolic act by the religious group Oomoto to emphasize their spiritual authority and connection to Japan's ancient religious traditions. Specifically, members of Oomoto collected sacred elements—fire, water, and earth—from [[Izumo-taisha]] during a pilgrimage. They then combined these elements with water from Moto-Ise, a site revered as the original location of the Ise Shrine and associated with the goddess Amaterasu. By mixing these sacred substances, Oomoto was asserting a deep and direct link to the ancient and most sacred sites of Shinto, effectively positioning themselves as a leading advocate for Japan's traditional spiritual practices.<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=v44BEAAAQBAJ&dq=%22Moto+Ise%22&pg=PA62|title=Prophet Motive: Deguchi Onisaburō, Oomoto, and the Rise of New Religions in Imperial Japan|last=Stalker|first=Nancy K.|date=2007-10-31|publisher=University of Hawaii Press|isbn=978-0-8248-6404-0|language=en|qq=draft}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Nao Deguchi A Biography of the Foundress of Oomoto|url=https://www.oomoto.or.jp/English/enKyos/kaisoden/index.html|access-date=2024-05-05|website=www.oomoto.or.jp}}</ref> Their headquarters are near this "Moto-Ise"<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=xlG3F6gSm9UC&dq=%22Moto+Ise%22&pg=PA232|title=Historical Dictionary of Shinto|last=Picken|first=Stuart D. B.|date=2010-12-28|publisher=Scarecrow Press|isbn=978-0-8108-7372-8|language=en}}</ref>.

[[File:Hibara-jinja,_torii_closeup.jpg|link=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Hibara-jinja,_torii_closeup.jpg|thumb|Miwa Torii demonstrating both their threefold nature and the closed gate]] {{ill|Moto-Ise Shrines|ja|元伊勢|1=Moto-Ise Shrines|fr|Sanctuaires Moto-Ise|en:draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Moto-Ise Shrines|13=User:Immanuelle/Moto-Ise Shrines|qq=}} are [[Shinto shrines]] that used to host Amaterasu before she was moved to [[Ise Grand Shrine|Ise Jingu]].<ref>{{Cite book |last=Kidder |first=J. Edward |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=7pEOicqsjv0C&dq=%22Moto-Ise%22&pg=PA201 |title=Himiko and Japan's Elusive Chiefdom of Yamatai: Archaeology, History, and Mythology |date=2007-02-28 |publisher=University of Hawaii Press |isbn=978-0-8248-3035-9 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Stalker |first=Nancy K. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=v44BEAAAQBAJ&dq=%22Moto-Ise%22&pg=PA62 |title=Prophet Motive: Deguchi Onisaburō, Oomoto, and the Rise of New Religions in Imperial Japan |date=2007-10-31 |publisher=University of Hawaii Press |isbn=978-0-8248-6404-0 |language=en}}</ref><ref name="iUniverse">{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=nPaezHFlfNQC&dq=%22Moto+Ise%22&pg=PT107|title=Where the Trees Grow Thick|publisher=iUniverse|isbn=978-0-595-28240-1|language=en}}</ref><ref name="Göttler-2017">{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=uyk_DwAAQBAJ&dq=%22Moto+Ise%22&pg=PA437|title=The Nomadic Object: The Challenge of World for Early Modern Religious Art|last1=Göttler|first1=Christine|last2=Mochizuki|first2=Mia|date=2017-11-06|publisher=BRILL|isbn=978-90-04-35450-0|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=PvgsAAAAIAAJ&dq=%22Moto+Ise%22&pg=RA3-PA147|title=Pamphlet - Dept. of the Army|last=Army|first=United States Department of the|date=1945|publisher=Headquarters, Department of the Army.|language=en}}</ref><ref name="Dougill-2023">{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=-H_cEAAAQBAJ&dq=%22Moto+Ise%22&pg=PT204|title=Off the Beaten Tracks in Japan: A Journey by Train from Hokkaido to Kyushu|last=Dougill|first=John|date=2023-11-07|publisher=Stone Bridge Press, Inc.|isbn=978-1-61172-963-4|language=en}}</ref> The first one was [[:en:Ōmiwa Shrine|Hibara Shrine]] (a subshrine of [[:en:Ōmiwa Shrine|Ōmiwa Shrine]]).<ref name="greenshinto">{{Cite web |last=D |first=John |date=2011-08-10 |title=Hibara Jinja and Amaterasu |url=https://www.greenshinto.com/2011/08/11/hibara-jinja-and-amaterasu/ |access-date=2023-10-18 |website=Green Shinto |language=en-GB}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Hibara Jinja Shrine（Nara） |url=https://www.jldb.bunka.go.jp/en/location/290100006/?search=1&q=Hibara+Shrine |access-date=2023-10-03 |website=Nationwide location database |language=en}}</ref><ref name="YAMATO UNKNOWN ORIGIN">{{Cite web |title=Omiwa Jinja Shrine/Sai Jinja Shrine/Kuehiko Jinja Shrine/Hibara Jinja Shrine│Destinations│Discover YAMATO│YAMATO UNKNOWN ORIGIN |url=http://www.city.sakurai.lg.jp/section/yamato-travel/destination/area01/spot02/ |access-date=2023-10-03 |website=YAMATO UNKNOWN ORIGIN |language=en}}</ref> Amaterasu was originally enshrined there before eventually moving to other Moto-Ise shrines and then finally to [[Ise Grand Shrine|Ise Jingu]].<ref name="YAMATO UNKNOWN ORIGIN" /><ref name="iUniverse" /><ref name="Göttler-2017" /><ref name="Dougill-2023" />
The journey was long so many shrines claim this title.<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=7pEOicqsjv0C&dq=%22Moto+Ise%22&pg=PA201|title=Himiko and Japan's Elusive Chiefdom of Yamatai: Archaeology, History, and Mythology|last=Kidder|first=J. Edward|date=2007-02-28|publisher=University of Hawaii Press|isbn=978-0-8248-3035-9|language=en}}</ref> These shrines are subject to a large amount of historical research.<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=XEIiEAAAQBAJ&dq=%22Moto+Ise%22&pg=PA534|title=RLE: Japan Mini-Set F: Philosophy and Religion (4 vols)|last=Authors|first=Various|date=2021-03-18|publisher=Routledge|isbn=978-1-136-90356-4|language=en}}</ref>
== Hibara Shrine == '''Hibara Shrine''' is a subshrine of Omiwa Shrine at the foot of {{ill|10=en|11=Mount_Miwa|12=fr|13=Mont Miwa|Mount Miwa|lt=Mount Miwa|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/10=en|qq=}} in [[Sakurai, Nara|Sakurai]], [[Nara Prefecture]]. The shrine is identified as the place where the {{ill|10=en|11=Yata-no-Kagami|Yata-no-Kagami|lt=Yata-no-Kagami|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/10=en|qq=}} and the {{ill|10=en|11=Kusanagi no Tsurugi|lt=Kusanagi-no-Tsurugi|Kusanagi no Tsurugi|lt=Kusanagi no Tsurugi|lt=Kusanagi-no-Tsurugi|lt=Kusanagi no Tsurugi|lt=Kusanagi-no-Tsurugi|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/10=en|qq=}} were first enshrined after they were removed from the imperial palace. It is the first of many {{ill|Moto-Ise Shrines|lt=Moto-Ise|ja|元伊勢|1=Moto-Ise Shrines|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Moto-Ise Shrines|13=User:Immanuelle/Moto-Ise Shrines|qq=}} shrines<ref name="greenshinto2">{{Cite web|last=D|first=John|date=2011-08-10|title=Hibara Jinja and Amaterasu|url=https://www.greenshinto.com/2011/08/11/hibara-jinja-and-amaterasu/|access-date=2023-10-18|website=Green Shinto|language=en-GB}}</ref>.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Hibara Jinja Shrine（Nara）|url=https://www.jldb.bunka.go.jp/en/location/290100006/?search=1&q=Hibara+Shrine|access-date=2023-10-03|website=Nationwide location database|language=en}}</ref><ref name="YAMATO UNKNOWN ORIGIN-2">{{Cite web|title=Omiwa Jinja Shrine/Sai Jinja Shrine/Kuehiko Jinja Shrine/Hibara Jinja Shrine│Destinations│Discover YAMATO│YAMATO UNKNOWN ORIGIN|url=http://www.city.sakurai.lg.jp/section/yamato-travel/destination/area01/spot02/|access-date=2023-10-03|website=YAMATO UNKNOWN ORIGIN|language=en}}</ref> Amaterasu was originally enshrined there before eventually moving to other Moto-Ise shrines and then finally to [[Ise Grand Shrine|Ise Jingu]].<ref name="YAMATO UNKNOWN ORIGIN-2" /> It has an [[Iwakura rock]] and a Shinza made of [[Sakaki]] wood.<ref name="YAMATO UNKNOWN ORIGIN-2" />
It has a prominent unique closable triple [[torii]] gate.<ref name="greenshinto2" />
== Summary == The deity enshrined at the Inner Shrine (内宮) of Ise Jingu (伊勢神宮), [[Amaterasu|Amaterasu Omikami]] (天照大御神), is considered the [[Oyagami|ancestral deity]] (皇祖神) of the emperors. Up until the era of the 10th Emperor, [[:en:Emperor Sujin|Emperor Sujin]] (崇神天皇), it is said that the emperor and Amaterasu Omikami shared the same residence, known as "sharing the same bed and palace" (同床共殿). Initially, she was enshrined within the [[Tokyo Imperial Palace|Imperial Palace]] (皇居), but fearing this arrangement, the emperor entrusted her divine spirit to Princess {{ill|Toyosukiiri-hime|ja|豊鍬入姫命|en:draft|simple|User:Immanuelle/Toyosukiiri-hime|fr|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Toyosukiiri-hime|qq=}} (豊鋤入姫命)<ref name="iUniverse" />, who established a sacred fence known as the "Iseki-no-himorogi" (磯城の神籬) in Iseshiro, Kasafu village (笠縫邑), [[Yamato Province|Yamato province]] (倭国). This began a search for an ideal location for her permanent enshrinement, which led to several relocations. Eventually, the 11th Emperor, [[:en:Emperor Suinin|Emperor Suijin]]'s (垂仁天皇) fourth princess, Princess [[:en:Yamatohime-no-mikoto|Yamatohime-no-mikoto]] (倭姫命), took over this mission, and after approximately 90 years, the shrine was moved to its current location.<ref name="iUniverse" /><ref name="Dougill-2023" /> The "Iseki-no-himorogi" is first mentioned during the relocation of Amaterasu Omikami to Yamato Kasafu village in the Chronicles of Emperor Suinin, where it is imagined as a facility for the placement of a {{ill|Mirrors in Shinto|lt=Mirrors in Shinto|lt=Shinto mirror|lt=divine mirror|simple|User:Immanuelle/Shinto mirror|en|Mirrors in Shinto|fr|Miroirs dans le shintoïsme|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinto mirror|qq=}}, symbolizing a sacred area akin to a rock seat, with a vast horizontal landscape preserving the tradition of the Iseshiro form. At Ise Jingu, the Shin-no-mihashira (心御柱), a central sacred pillar, is largely buried in the ground with its surroundings wrapped in sakaki (榊), and ritual pottery symbolizes the rituals. It is said that when the divine mirror of Amaterasu Omikami was first dedicated, a five-hundred-year-old tree from {{ill|Mount Amanokagu|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mount Amanokagu|qq=}} was dug up, with jewels hung on its upper branches and a mirror on its middle branches, but the sakaki-decorated Shin-no-mihashira symbolizes the appearance of this sacred tree during rituals. The relocation process is not mentioned in the "[[Kojiki]]," but is briefly noted in the "[[Nihon Shoki]]," more detailed in the "{{ill|Kotai Jingu Gishiki|ja|皇太神宮儀式帳|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kotai Jingu Gishiki|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 延暦儀式帳}}," and most elaborately in the "{{ill|Yamatohime-no-mikoto Seiki|ja|倭姫命世記|1=Yamatohime no Mikoto Seiki|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yamatohime-no-mikoto Seiki|13=User:Immanuelle/Yamatohime no Mikoto Seiki|qq=}}," a medieval text from the "{{ill|Shintō Gobusho|lt=Shintō Gobusho|lt=Shinto Gobusho|ja|神道五部書|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinto Gobusho|qq=}} (神道五部書)."
The deity of the Outer Shrine (外宮), [[Toyouke-hime|Toyouke-no-Ōmikami]] (豊受大御神), although not mentioned in the "[[Kojiki]]" or "[[Nihon Shoki]]," is said in the "{{ill|Toyuke Gū Gishiki|ja|止由気宮儀式帳|lt=Toyuke Shrine Ritual Book|lt_ja=止由気宮儀式帳|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Toyuke Gū Gishiki|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 延暦儀式帳}}" and "{{ill|Yamatohime-no-mikoto Seiki|ja|倭姫命世記|lt=Yamatohime-no-mikoto Chronicles|lt_ja=倭姫命世記|1=Yamatohime no Mikoto Seiki|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yamatohime-no-mikoto Seiki|13=User:Immanuelle/Yamatohime no Mikoto Seiki|qq=}}" to have been relocated from Tango Province (丹後国) (now part of Tanba Province (丹波国)) to her current site by divine command of Amaterasu Omikami during the era of the 21st Emperor, Emperor Yūryaku (雄略天皇).
The tale of Amaterasu Omikami's wanderings is considered similar to the ancestral deity stories in the "{{ill|Hitachi Province Fudoki|ja|常陸国風土記|zh|常陸國風土記|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hitachi Province Fudoki|qq=}}" about {{ill|Mount Tsukuba|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mount Tsukuba|qq=}} (筑波山) and the folk tales about {{ill|Kūkai|4=en|6=fr|8=ja|9=弘法大師|10=simple|11=User:Immanuelle/Kūkai|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kūkai|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 空海}} (弘法大師). Since many shrine origin stories involve deities traveling to find their enshrinement locations, this is considered a typical motif of a "traveling deity."
The origin tradition of the "Former Ise" is derived from texts like the "{{ill|Kotai Jingu Gishiki|ja|皇太神宮儀式帳|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kotai Jingu Gishiki|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 延暦儀式帳}}, {{ill|Toyuke Gū Gishiki|ja|止由気宮儀式帳|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Toyuke Gū Gishiki|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 延暦儀式帳}}, {{ill|Kogo Shūi|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kogo Shūi|qq=}}, and [[Engishiki]]." Although it was previously said to involve around twenty locations, it now includes over sixty. These traditions are based on those transmitted to various shrines, and there are cases where nearby locations claim to be the traditional site, leaving the truth of these claims unclear.
==Oomoto== A Moto-Ise Shrine "North of {{ill|Ayabe, Kyoto|lt=Ayabe|en|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ayabe, Kyoto|qq=}}", {{ill|Amanoiwato Shrine|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Amanoiwato Shrine|qq=}} was used in a symbolic act by the religious group Oomoto to emphasize their spiritual authority and connection to Japan's ancient religious traditions. Specifically, members of Oomoto collected sacred elements—fire, water, and earth—from [[Izumo-taisha]] during a pilgrimage. They then combined these elements with water from Moto-Ise, a site revered as the original location of the Ise Shrine and associated with the goddess Amaterasu. By mixing these sacred substances, Oomoto was asserting a deep and direct link to the ancient and most sacred sites of Shinto, effectively positioning themselves as a leading advocate for Japan's traditional spiritual practices.<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=v44BEAAAQBAJ&dq=%22Moto+Ise%22&pg=PA62|title=Prophet Motive: Deguchi Onisaburō, Oomoto, and the Rise of New Religions in Imperial Japan|last=Stalker|first=Nancy K.|date=2007-10-31|publisher=University of Hawaii Press|isbn=978-0-8248-6404-0|language=en|qq=draft}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Nao Deguchi A Biography of the Foundress of Oomoto|url=https://www.oomoto.or.jp/English/enKyos/kaisoden/index.html|access-date=2024-05-05|website=www.oomoto.or.jp}}</ref> Their headquarters are near this "Moto-Ise"<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=xlG3F6gSm9UC&dq=%22Moto+Ise%22&pg=PA232|title=Historical Dictionary of Shinto|last=Picken|first=Stuart D. B.|date=2010-12-28|publisher=Scarecrow Press|isbn=978-0-8108-7372-8|language=en}}</ref>.

The journey was long so many shrines claim this title.<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=7pEOicqsjv0C&dq=%22Moto+Ise%22&pg=PA201|title=Himiko and Japan's Elusive Chiefdom of Yamatai: Archaeology, History, and Mythology|last=Kidder|first=J. Edward|date=2007-02-28|publisher=University of Hawaii Press|isbn=978-0-8248-3035-9|language=en}}</ref> These shrines are subject to a large amount of historical research.<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=XEIiEAAAQBAJ&dq=%22Moto+Ise%22&pg=PA534|title=RLE: Japan Mini-Set F: Philosophy and Religion (4 vols)|last=Authors|first=Various|date=2021-03-18|publisher=Routledge|isbn=978-1-136-90356-4|language=en}}</ref>
== Hibara Shrine == '''Hibara Shrine''' is a subshrine of Omiwa Shrine at the foot of {{ill|10=en|11=Mount_Miwa|12=fr|13=Mont Miwa|Mount Miwa|lt=Mount Miwa|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/10=en|qq=}} in [[Sakurai, Nara|Sakurai]], [[:en:Nara Prefecture|Nara Prefecture]]. The shrine is identified as the place where the {{ill|10=en|11=Yata-no-Kagami|Yata-no-Kagami|lt=Yata-no-Kagami|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/10=en|qq=}} and the {{ill|10=en|11=Kusanagi no Tsurugi|lt=Kusanagi-no-Tsurugi|Kusanagi no Tsurugi|lt=Kusanagi no Tsurugi|lt=Kusanagi-no-Tsurugi|lt=Kusanagi no Tsurugi|lt=Kusanagi-no-Tsurugi|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/10=en|qq=}} were first enshrined after they were removed from the imperial palace. It is the first of many {{ill|Moto-Ise Shrines|lt=Moto-Ise|ja|元伊勢|1=Moto-Ise Shrines|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Moto-Ise Shrines|13=User:Immanuelle/Moto-Ise Shrines|qq=}} shrines<ref name="greenshinto2">{{Cite web|last=D|first=John|date=2011-08-10|title=Hibara Jinja and Amaterasu|url=https://www.greenshinto.com/2011/08/11/hibara-jinja-and-amaterasu/|access-date=2023-10-18|website=Green Shinto|language=en-GB}}</ref>.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Hibara Jinja Shrine（Nara）|url=https://www.jldb.bunka.go.jp/en/location/290100006/?search=1&q=Hibara+Shrine|access-date=2023-10-03|website=Nationwide location database|language=en}}</ref><ref name="YAMATO UNKNOWN ORIGIN-2">{{Cite web|title=Omiwa Jinja Shrine/Sai Jinja Shrine/Kuehiko Jinja Shrine/Hibara Jinja Shrine│Destinations│Discover YAMATO│YAMATO UNKNOWN ORIGIN|url=http://www.city.sakurai.lg.jp/section/yamato-travel/destination/area01/spot02/|access-date=2023-10-03|website=YAMATO UNKNOWN ORIGIN|language=en}}</ref> Amaterasu was originally enshrined there before eventually moving to other Moto-Ise shrines and then finally to [[Ise Grand Shrine|Ise Jingu]].<ref name="YAMATO UNKNOWN ORIGIN-2" /> It has an [[Iwakura rock]] and a Shinza made of [[Sakaki]] wood.<ref name="YAMATO UNKNOWN ORIGIN-2" />
It has a prominent unique closable triple [[torii]] gate.<ref name="greenshinto2" />
== Summary == The deity enshrined at the Inner Shrine (内宮) of Ise Jingu (伊勢神宮), [[Amaterasu|Amaterasu Omikami]] (天照大御神), is considered the [[Oyagami|ancestral deity]] (皇祖神) of the emperors. Up until the era of the 10th Emperor, [[:en:Emperor Sujin|Emperor Sujin]] (崇神天皇), it is said that the emperor and Amaterasu Omikami shared the same residence, known as "sharing the same bed and palace" (同床共殿). Initially, she was enshrined within the [[Tokyo Imperial Palace|Imperial Palace]] (皇居), but fearing this arrangement, the emperor entrusted her divine spirit to Princess {{ill|Toyosukiiri-hime|ja|豊鍬入姫命|en:draft|simple|User:Immanuelle/Toyosukiiri-hime|fr|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Toyosukiiri-hime|qq=}} (豊鋤入姫命)<ref name="iUniverse" />, who established a sacred fence known as the "Iseki-no-himorogi" (磯城の神籬) in Iseshiro, Kasafu village (笠縫邑), [[Yamato Province|Yamato province]] (倭国). This began a search for an ideal location for her permanent enshrinement, which led to several relocations. Eventually, the 11th Emperor, [[:en:Emperor Suinin|Emperor Suijin]]'s (垂仁天皇) fourth princess, Princess [[:en:Yamatohime-no-mikoto|Yamatohime-no-mikoto]] (倭姫命), took over this mission, and after approximately 90 years, the shrine was moved to its current location.<ref name="iUniverse" /><ref name="Dougill-2023" /> The "Iseki-no-himorogi" is first mentioned during the relocation of Amaterasu Omikami to Yamato Kasafu village in the Chronicles of Emperor Suinin, where it is imagined as a facility for the placement of a {{ill|Mirrors in Shinto|lt=Mirrors in Shinto|lt=Shinto mirror|lt=divine mirror|simple|User:Immanuelle/Shinto mirror|en|Mirrors in Shinto|fr|Miroirs dans le shintoïsme|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinto mirror|qq=}}, symbolizing a sacred area akin to a rock seat, with a vast horizontal landscape preserving the tradition of the Iseshiro form. At Ise Jingu, the Shin-no-mihashira (心御柱), a central sacred pillar, is largely buried in the ground with its surroundings wrapped in sakaki (榊), and ritual pottery symbolizes the rituals. It is said that when the divine mirror of Amaterasu Omikami was first dedicated, a five-hundred-year-old tree from {{ill|Mount Amanokagu|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mount Amanokagu|qq=}} was dug up, with jewels hung on its upper branches and a mirror on its middle branches, but the sakaki-decorated Shin-no-mihashira symbolizes the appearance of this sacred tree during rituals. The relocation process is not mentioned in the "[[Kojiki]]," but is briefly noted in the "[[Nihon Shoki]]," more detailed in the "{{ill|Kotai Jingu Gishiki|ja|皇太神宮儀式帳|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kotai Jingu Gishiki|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 延暦儀式帳}}," and most elaborately in the "{{ill|Yamatohime-no-mikoto Seiki|ja|倭姫命世記|1=Yamatohime no Mikoto Seiki|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yamatohime-no-mikoto Seiki|13=User:Immanuelle/Yamatohime no Mikoto Seiki|qq=}}," a medieval text from the "{{ill|Shintō Gobusho|lt=Shintō Gobusho|lt=Shinto Gobusho|ja|神道五部書|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinto Gobusho|qq=}} (神道五部書)."
The deity of the Outer Shrine (外宮), [[Toyouke-hime|Toyouke-no-Ōmikami]] (豊受大御神), although not mentioned in the "[[Kojiki]]" or "[[Nihon Shoki]]," is said in the "{{ill|Toyuke Gū Gishiki|ja|止由気宮儀式帳|lt=Toyuke Shrine Ritual Book|lt_ja=止由気宮儀式帳|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Toyuke Gū Gishiki|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 延暦儀式帳}}" and "{{ill|Yamatohime-no-mikoto Seiki|ja|倭姫命世記|lt=Yamatohime-no-mikoto Chronicles|lt_ja=倭姫命世記|1=Yamatohime no Mikoto Seiki|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yamatohime-no-mikoto Seiki|13=User:Immanuelle/Yamatohime no Mikoto Seiki|qq=}}" to have been relocated from Tango Province (丹後国) (now part of Tanba Province (丹波国)) to her current site by divine command of Amaterasu Omikami during the era of the 21st Emperor, Emperor Yūryaku (雄略天皇).
The tale of Amaterasu Omikami's wanderings is considered similar to the ancestral deity stories in the "{{ill|Hitachi Province Fudoki|ja|常陸国風土記|zh|常陸國風土記|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hitachi Province Fudoki|qq=}}" about {{ill|Mount Tsukuba|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mount Tsukuba|qq=}} (筑波山) and the folk tales about {{ill|Kūkai|4=en|6=fr|8=ja|9=弘法大師|10=simple|11=User:Immanuelle/Kūkai|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kūkai|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 空海}} (弘法大師). Since many shrine origin stories involve deities traveling to find their enshrinement locations, this is considered a typical motif of a "traveling deity."
The origin tradition of the "Former Ise" is derived from texts like the "{{ill|Kotai Jingu Gishiki|ja|皇太神宮儀式帳|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kotai Jingu Gishiki|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 延暦儀式帳}}, {{ill|Toyuke Gū Gishiki|ja|止由気宮儀式帳|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Toyuke Gū Gishiki|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 延暦儀式帳}}, {{ill|Kogo Shūi|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kogo Shūi|qq=}}, and [[Engishiki]]." Although it was previously said to involve around twenty locations, it now includes over sixty. These traditions are based on those transmitted to various shrines, and there are cases where nearby locations claim to be the traditional site, leaving the truth of these claims unclear.
==Oomoto== A Moto-Ise Shrine "North of {{ill|Ayabe, Kyoto|lt=Ayabe|en|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ayabe, Kyoto|qq=}}", {{ill|Amanoiwato Shrine|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Amanoiwato Shrine|qq=}} was used in a symbolic act by the religious group Oomoto to emphasize their spiritual authority and connection to Japan's ancient religious traditions. Specifically, members of Oomoto collected sacred elements—fire, water, and earth—from [[Izumo-taisha]] during a pilgrimage. They then combined these elements with water from Moto-Ise, a site revered as the original location of the Ise Shrine and associated with the goddess Amaterasu. By mixing these sacred substances, Oomoto was asserting a deep and direct link to the ancient and most sacred sites of Shinto, effectively positioning themselves as a leading advocate for Japan's traditional spiritual practices.<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=v44BEAAAQBAJ&dq=%22Moto+Ise%22&pg=PA62|title=Prophet Motive: Deguchi Onisaburō, Oomoto, and the Rise of New Religions in Imperial Japan|last=Stalker|first=Nancy K.|date=2007-10-31|publisher=University of Hawaii Press|isbn=978-0-8248-6404-0|language=en|qq=draft}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Nao Deguchi A Biography of the Foundress of Oomoto|url=https://www.oomoto.or.jp/English/enKyos/kaisoden/index.html|access-date=2024-05-05|website=www.oomoto.or.jp}}</ref> Their headquarters are near this "Moto-Ise"<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=xlG3F6gSm9UC&dq=%22Moto+Ise%22&pg=PA232|title=Historical Dictionary of Shinto|last=Picken|first=Stuart D. B.|date=2010-12-28|publisher=Scarecrow Press|isbn=978-0-8108-7372-8|language=en}}</ref>.
