Edward|date=2007-02-28|publisher=University of Hawaii Press|isbn=978-0-8248-3035-9|language=en}}</ref> These shrines are subject to a large amount of historical research.<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=XEIiEAAAQBAJ&dq=%22Moto+Ise%22&pg=PA534|title=RLE: Japan Mini-Set F: Philosophy and Religion (4 vols)|last=Authors|first=Various|date=2021-03-18|publisher=Routledge|isbn=978-1-136-90356-4|language=en}}</ref>
== Hibara Shrine == '''Hibara Shrine''' is a subshrine of Omiwa Shrine at the foot of {{ill|10=en|11=Mount_Miwa|12=fr|13=Mont Miwa|Mount Miwa|lt=Mount Miwa|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/10=en|qq=}} in [[:en:Sakurai, Nara|Sakurai]], [[:en:Nara Prefecture|Nara Prefecture]]. The shrine is identified as the place where the {{ill|10=en|11=Yata-no-Kagami|Yata-no-Kagami|lt=Yata-no-Kagami|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/10=en|qq=}} and the {{ill|10=en|11=Kusanagi no Tsurugi|lt=Kusanagi-no-Tsurugi|Kusanagi no Tsurugi|lt=Kusanagi no Tsurugi|lt=Kusanagi-no-Tsurugi|lt=Kusanagi no Tsurugi|lt=Kusanagi-no-Tsurugi|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/10=en|qq=}} were first enshrined after they were removed from the imperial palace. It is the first of many {{ill|Moto-Ise Shrines|lt=Moto-Ise|ja|元伊勢|1=Moto-Ise Shrines|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Moto-Ise Shrines|13=User:Immanuelle/Moto-Ise Shrines|qq=}} shrines<ref name="greenshinto2">{{Cite web|last=D|first=John|date=2011-08-10|title=Hibara Jinja and Amaterasu|url=https://www.greenshinto.com/2011/08/11/hibara-jinja-and-amaterasu/|access-date=2023-10-18|website=Green Shinto|language=en-GB}}</ref>.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Hibara Jinja Shrine（Nara）|url=https://www.jldb.bunka.go.jp/en/location/290100006/?search=1&q=Hibara+Shrine|access-date=2023-10-03|website=Nationwide location database|language=en}}</ref><ref name="YAMATO UNKNOWN ORIGIN-2">{{Cite web|title=Omiwa Jinja Shrine/Sai Jinja Shrine/Kuehiko Jinja Shrine/Hibara Jinja Shrine│Destinations│Discover YAMATO│YAMATO UNKNOWN ORIGIN|url=http://www.city.sakurai.lg.jp/section/yamato-travel/destination/area01/spot02/|access-date=2023-10-03|website=YAMATO UNKNOWN ORIGIN|language=en}}</ref> Amaterasu was originally enshrined there before eventually moving to other Moto-Ise shrines and then finally to [[Ise Grand Shrine|Ise Jingu]].<ref name="YAMATO UNKNOWN ORIGIN-2" /> It has an [[Iwakura rock]] and a Shinza made of [[:en:Cleyera japonica|Cleyera japonica]] wood.<ref name="YAMATO UNKNOWN ORIGIN-2" />
It has a prominent unique closable triple [[torii]] gate.<ref name="greenshinto2" />
== Summary == The deity enshrined at the Inner Shrine (内宮) of Ise Jingu (伊勢神宮), [[Amaterasu|Amaterasu Omikami]] (天照大御神), is considered the [[Oyagami|ancestral deity]] (皇祖神) of the emperors. Up until the era of the 10th Emperor, [[:en:Emperor Sujin|Emperor Sujin]] (崇神天皇), it is said that the emperor and Amaterasu Omikami shared the same residence, known as "sharing the same bed and palace" (同床共殿). Initially, she was enshrined within the [[Tokyo Imperial Palace|Imperial Palace]] (皇居), but fearing this arrangement, the emperor entrusted her divine spirit to Princess {{ill|Toyosukiiri-hime|ja|豊鍬入姫命|en:draft|simple|User:Immanuelle/Toyosukiiri-hime|fr|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Toyosukiiri-hime|qq=}} (豊鋤入姫命)<ref name="iUniverse" />, who established a sacred fence known as the "Iseki-no-himorogi" (磯城の神籬) in Iseshiro, Kasafu village (笠縫邑), [[:en:Yamato Province|Yamato province]] (倭国). This began a search for an ideal location for her permanent enshrinement, which led to several relocations. Eventually, the 11th Emperor, [[:en:Emperor Suinin|Emperor Suijin]]'s (垂仁天皇) fourth princess, Princess [[:en:Yamatohime-no-mikoto|Yamatohime-no-mikoto]] (倭姫命), took over this mission, and after approximately 90 years, the shrine was moved to its current location.<ref name="iUniverse" /><ref name="Dougill-2023" /> The "Iseki-no-himorogi" is first mentioned during the relocation of Amaterasu Omikami to Yamato Kasafu village in the Chronicles of Emperor Suinin, where it is imagined as a facility for the placement of a {{ill|Mirrors in Shinto|lt=Mirrors in Shinto|lt=Shinto mirror|lt=divine mirror|simple|User:Immanuelle/Shinto mirror|en|Mirrors in Shinto|fr|Miroirs dans le shintoïsme|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinto mirror|qq=}}, symbolizing a sacred area akin to a rock seat, with a vast horizontal landscape preserving the tradition of the Iseshiro form. At Ise Jingu, the Shin-no-mihashira (心御柱), a central sacred pillar, is largely buried in the ground with its surroundings wrapped in sakaki (榊), and ritual pottery symbolizes the rituals. It is said that when the divine mirror of Amaterasu Omikami was first dedicated, a five-hundred-year-old tree from {{ill|Mount Amanokagu|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mount Amanokagu|qq=}} was dug up, with jewels hung on its upper branches and a mirror on its middle branches, but the sakaki-decorated Shin-no-mihashira symbolizes the appearance of this sacred tree during rituals. The relocation process is not mentioned in the "[[Kojiki]]," but is briefly noted in the "[[Nihon Shoki]]," more detailed in the "{{ill|Kotai Jingu Gishiki|ja|皇太神宮儀式帳|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kotai Jingu Gishiki|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 延暦儀式帳|1=Enryaku Gishikichō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q109596938}}," and most elaborately in the "{{ill|Yamatohime-no-mikoto Seiki|ja|倭姫命世記|1=Yamatohime no Mikoto Seiki|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yamatohime-no-mikoto Seiki|13=User:Immanuelle/Yamatohime no Mikoto Seiki|qq=}}," a medieval text from the "{{ill|Shintō Gobusho|lt=Shintō Gobusho|lt=Shinto Gobusho|ja|神道五部書|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinto Gobusho|qq=}} (神道五部書)."
The deity of the Outer Shrine (外宮), [[:en:Toyouke-hime|Toyouke-no-Ōmikami]] (豊受大御神), although not mentioned in the "[[Kojiki]]" or "[[Nihon Shoki]]," is said in the "{{ill|Toyuke Gū Gishiki|ja|止由気宮儀式帳|lt=Toyuke Shrine Ritual Book|lt_ja=止由気宮儀式帳|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Toyuke Gū Gishiki|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 延暦儀式帳|1=Enryaku Gishikichō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q109596938}}" and "{{ill|Yamatohime-no-mikoto Seiki|ja|倭姫命世記|lt=Yamatohime-no-mikoto Chronicles|lt_ja=倭姫命世記|1=Yamatohime no Mikoto Seiki|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yamatohime-no-mikoto Seiki|13=User:Immanuelle/Yamatohime no Mikoto Seiki|qq=}}" to have been relocated from Tango Province (丹後国) (now part of Tanba Province (丹波国)) to her current site by divine command of Amaterasu Omikami during the era of the 21st Emperor, Emperor Yūryaku (雄略天皇).
The tale of Amaterasu Omikami's wanderings is considered similar to the ancestral deity stories in the "{{ill|Hitachi Province Fudoki|ja|常陸国風土記|zh|常陸國風土記|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hitachi Province Fudoki|qq=|1=Hitachi no Kuni Fudoki|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11481687}}" about {{ill|Mount Tsukuba|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mount Tsukuba|qq=}} (筑波山) and the folk tales about {{ill|Kūkai|4=en|6=fr|8=ja|9=弘法大師|10=simple|11=User:Immanuelle/Kūkai|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kūkai|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 空海|1=Kūkai|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q222227}} (弘法大師). Since many shrine origin stories involve deities traveling to find their enshrinement locations, this is considered a typical motif of a "traveling deity."
The origin tradition of the "Former Ise" is derived from texts like the "{{ill|Kotai Jingu Gishiki|ja|皇太神宮儀式帳|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kotai Jingu Gishiki|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 延暦儀式帳|1=Enryaku Gishikichō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q109596938}}, {{ill|Toyuke Gū Gishiki|ja|止由気宮儀式帳|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Toyuke Gū Gishiki|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 延暦儀式帳|1=Enryaku Gishikichō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q109596938}}, {{ill|Kogo Shūi|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kogo Shūi|qq=}}, and [[Engishiki]]." Although it was previously said to involve around twenty locations, it now includes over sixty. These traditions are based on those transmitted to various shrines, and there are cases where nearby locations claim to be the traditional site, leaving the truth of these claims unclear.
==Oomoto== A Moto-Ise Shrine "North of {{ill|Ayabe, Kyoto|lt=Ayabe|en|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ayabe, Kyoto|qq=}}", {{ill|Amanoiwato Shrine|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Amanoiwato Shrine|qq=}} was used in a symbolic act by the religious group Oomoto to emphasize their spiritual authority and connection to Japan's ancient religious traditions. Specifically, members of Oomoto collected sacred elements—fire, water, and earth—from [[Izumo-taisha]] during a pilgrimage. They then combined these elements with water from Moto-Ise, a site revered as the original location of the Ise Shrine and associated with the goddess Amaterasu. By mixing these sacred substances, Oomoto was asserting a deep and direct link to the ancient and most sacred sites of Shinto, effectively positioning themselves as a leading advocate for Japan's traditional spiritual practices.<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=v44BEAAAQBAJ&dq=%22Moto+Ise%22&pg=PA62|title=Prophet Motive: Deguchi Onisaburō, Oomoto, and the Rise of New Religions in Imperial Japan|last=Stalker|first=Nancy K.|date=2007-10-31|publisher=University of Hawaii Press|isbn=978-0-8248-6404-0|language=en|qq=draft}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Nao Deguchi A Biography of the Foundress of Oomoto|url=https://www.oomoto.or.jp/English/enKyos/kaisoden/index.html|access-date=2024-05-05|website=www.oomoto.or.jp}}</ref> Their headquarters are near this "Moto-Ise"<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=xlG3F6gSm9UC&dq=%22Moto+Ise%22&pg=PA232|title=Historical Dictionary of Shinto|last=Picken|first=Stuart D. B.|date=2010-12-28|publisher=Scarecrow Press|isbn=978-0-8108-7372-8|language=en}}</ref>.

Dept. of the Army|last=Army|first=United States Department of the|date=1945|publisher=Headquarters, Department of the Army.|language=en}}</ref><ref name="Dougill-2023">{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=-H_cEAAAQBAJ&dq=%22Moto+Ise%22&pg=PT204|title=Off the Beaten Tracks in Japan: A Journey by Train from Hokkaido to Kyushu|last=Dougill|first=John|date=2023-11-07|publisher=Stone Bridge Press, Inc.|isbn=978-1-61172-963-4|language=en}}</ref> The first one was [[:en:Ōmiwa Shrine|Hibara Shrine]] (a subshrine of [[:en:Ōmiwa Shrine|Ōmiwa Shrine]]).<ref name="greenshinto">{{Cite web |last=D |first=John |date=2011-08-10 |title=Hibara Jinja and Amaterasu |url=https://www.greenshinto.com/2011/08/11/hibara-jinja-and-amaterasu/ |access-date=2023-10-18 |website=Green Shinto |language=en-GB}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Hibara Jinja Shrine（Nara） |url=https://www.jldb.bunka.go.jp/en/location/290100006/?search=1&q=Hibara+Shrine |access-date=2023-10-03 |website=Nationwide location database |language=en}}</ref><ref name="YAMATO UNKNOWN ORIGIN">{{Cite web |title=Omiwa Jinja Shrine/Sai Jinja Shrine/Kuehiko Jinja Shrine/Hibara Jinja Shrine│Destinations│Discover YAMATO│YAMATO UNKNOWN ORIGIN |url=http://www.city.sakurai.lg.jp/section/yamato-travel/destination/area01/spot02/ |access-date=2023-10-03 |website=YAMATO UNKNOWN ORIGIN |language=en}}</ref> Amaterasu was originally enshrined there before eventually moving to other Moto-Ise shrines and then finally to [[Ise Grand Shrine|Ise Jingu]].<ref name="YAMATO UNKNOWN ORIGIN" /><ref name="iUniverse" /><ref name="Göttler-2017" /><ref name="Dougill-2023" />
The journey was long so many shrines claim this title.<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=7pEOicqsjv0C&dq=%22Moto+Ise%22&pg=PA201|title=Himiko and Japan's Elusive Chiefdom of Yamatai: Archaeology, History, and Mythology|last=Kidder|first=J. Edward|date=2007-02-28|publisher=University of Hawaii Press|isbn=978-0-8248-3035-9|language=en}}</ref> These shrines are subject to a large amount of historical research.<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=XEIiEAAAQBAJ&dq=%22Moto+Ise%22&pg=PA534|title=RLE: Japan Mini-Set F: Philosophy and Religion (4 vols)|last=Authors|first=Various|date=2021-03-18|publisher=Routledge|isbn=978-1-136-90356-4|language=en}}</ref>
== Hibara Shrine == '''Hibara Shrine''' is a subshrine of Omiwa Shrine at the foot of {{ill|10=en|11=Mount_Miwa|12=fr|13=Mont Miwa|Mount Miwa|lt=Mount Miwa|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/10=en|qq=}} in [[:en:Sakurai, Nara|Sakurai]], [[:en:Nara Prefecture|Nara Prefecture]]. The shrine is identified as the place where the {{ill|10=en|11=Yata-no-Kagami|Yata-no-Kagami|lt=Yata-no-Kagami|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/10=en|qq=}} and the {{ill|10=en|11=Kusanagi no Tsurugi|lt=Kusanagi-no-Tsurugi|Kusanagi no Tsurugi|lt=Kusanagi no Tsurugi|lt=Kusanagi-no-Tsurugi|lt=Kusanagi no Tsurugi|lt=Kusanagi-no-Tsurugi|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/10=en|qq=}} were first enshrined after they were removed from the imperial palace. It is the first of many {{ill|Moto-Ise Shrines|lt=Moto-Ise|ja|元伊勢|1=Moto-Ise Shrines|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Moto-Ise Shrines|13=User:Immanuelle/Moto-Ise Shrines|qq=}} shrines<ref name="greenshinto2">{{Cite web|last=D|first=John|date=2011-08-10|title=Hibara Jinja and Amaterasu|url=https://www.greenshinto.com/2011/08/11/hibara-jinja-and-amaterasu/|access-date=2023-10-18|website=Green Shinto|language=en-GB}}</ref>.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Hibara Jinja Shrine（Nara）|url=https://www.jldb.bunka.go.jp/en/location/290100006/?search=1&q=Hibara+Shrine|access-date=2023-10-03|website=Nationwide location database|language=en}}</ref><ref name="YAMATO UNKNOWN ORIGIN-2">{{Cite web|title=Omiwa Jinja Shrine/Sai Jinja Shrine/Kuehiko Jinja Shrine/Hibara Jinja Shrine│Destinations│Discover YAMATO│YAMATO UNKNOWN ORIGIN|url=http://www.city.sakurai.lg.jp/section/yamato-travel/destination/area01/spot02/|access-date=2023-10-03|website=YAMATO UNKNOWN ORIGIN|language=en}}</ref> Amaterasu was originally enshrined there before eventually moving to other Moto-Ise shrines and then finally to [[Ise Grand Shrine|Ise Jingu]].<ref name="YAMATO UNKNOWN ORIGIN-2" /> It has an [[Iwakura rock]] and a Shinza made of [[:en:Cleyera japonica|Cleyera japonica]] wood.<ref name="YAMATO UNKNOWN ORIGIN-2" />
It has a prominent unique closable triple [[torii]] gate.<ref name="greenshinto2" />
== Summary == The deity enshrined at the Inner Shrine (内宮) of Ise Jingu (伊勢神宮), [[Amaterasu|Amaterasu Omikami]] (天照大御神), is considered the [[Oyagami|ancestral deity]] (皇祖神) of the emperors. Up until the era of the 10th Emperor, [[:en:Emperor Sujin|Emperor Sujin]] (崇神天皇), it is said that the emperor and Amaterasu Omikami shared the same residence, known as "sharing the same bed and palace" (同床共殿). Initially, she was enshrined within the [[Tokyo Imperial Palace|Imperial Palace]] (皇居), but fearing this arrangement, the emperor entrusted her divine spirit to Princess {{ill|Toyosukiiri-hime|ja|豊鍬入姫命|en:draft|simple|User:Immanuelle/Toyosukiiri-hime|fr|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Toyosukiiri-hime|qq=}} (豊鋤入姫命)<ref name="iUniverse" />, who established a sacred fence known as the "Iseki-no-himorogi" (磯城の神籬) in Iseshiro, Kasafu village (笠縫邑), [[:en:Yamato Province|Yamato province]] (倭国). This began a search for an ideal location for her permanent enshrinement, which led to several relocations. Eventually, the 11th Emperor, [[:en:Emperor Suinin|Emperor Suijin]]'s (垂仁天皇) fourth princess, Princess [[:en:Yamatohime-no-mikoto|Yamatohime-no-mikoto]] (倭姫命), took over this mission, and after approximately 90 years, the shrine was moved to its current location.<ref name="iUniverse" /><ref name="Dougill-2023" /> The "Iseki-no-himorogi" is first mentioned during the relocation of Amaterasu Omikami to Yamato Kasafu village in the Chronicles of Emperor Suinin, where it is imagined as a facility for the placement of a {{ill|Mirrors in Shinto|lt=Mirrors in Shinto|lt=Shinto mirror|lt=divine mirror|simple|User:Immanuelle/Shinto mirror|en|Mirrors in Shinto|fr|Miroirs dans le shintoïsme|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinto mirror|qq=}}, symbolizing a sacred area akin to a rock seat, with a vast horizontal landscape preserving the tradition of the Iseshiro form. At Ise Jingu, the Shin-no-mihashira (心御柱), a central sacred pillar, is largely buried in the ground with its surroundings wrapped in sakaki (榊), and ritual pottery symbolizes the rituals. It is said that when the divine mirror of Amaterasu Omikami was first dedicated, a five-hundred-year-old tree from {{ill|Mount Amanokagu|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mount Amanokagu|qq=}} was dug up, with jewels hung on its upper branches and a mirror on its middle branches, but the sakaki-decorated Shin-no-mihashira symbolizes the appearance of this sacred tree during rituals. The relocation process is not mentioned in the "[[Kojiki]]," but is briefly noted in the "[[Nihon Shoki]]," more detailed in the "{{ill|Kotai Jingu Gishiki|ja|皇太神宮儀式帳|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kotai Jingu Gishiki|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 延暦儀式帳|1=Enryaku Gishikichō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q109596938}}," and most elaborately in the "{{ill|Yamatohime-no-mikoto Seiki|ja|倭姫命世記|1=Yamatohime no Mikoto Seiki|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yamatohime-no-mikoto Seiki|13=User:Immanuelle/Yamatohime no Mikoto Seiki|qq=}}," a medieval text from the "{{ill|Shintō Gobusho|lt=Shintō Gobusho|lt=Shinto Gobusho|ja|神道五部書|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinto Gobusho|qq=}} (神道五部書)."
The deity of the Outer Shrine (外宮), [[:en:Toyouke-hime|Toyouke-no-Ōmikami]] (豊受大御神), although not mentioned in the "[[Kojiki]]" or "[[Nihon Shoki]]," is said in the "{{ill|Toyuke Gū Gishiki|ja|止由気宮儀式帳|lt=Toyuke Shrine Ritual Book|lt_ja=止由気宮儀式帳|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Toyuke Gū Gishiki|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 延暦儀式帳|1=Enryaku Gishikichō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q109596938}}" and "{{ill|Yamatohime-no-mikoto Seiki|ja|倭姫命世記|lt=Yamatohime-no-mikoto Chronicles|lt_ja=倭姫命世記|1=Yamatohime no Mikoto Seiki|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yamatohime-no-mikoto Seiki|13=User:Immanuelle/Yamatohime no Mikoto Seiki|qq=}}" to have been relocated from Tango Province (丹後国) (now part of Tanba Province (丹波国)) to her current site by divine command of Amaterasu Omikami during the era of the 21st Emperor, Emperor Yūryaku (雄略天皇).
The tale of Amaterasu Omikami's wanderings is considered similar to the ancestral deity stories in the "{{ill|Hitachi Province Fudoki|ja|常陸国風土記|zh|常陸國風土記|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hitachi Province Fudoki|qq=|1=Hitachi no Kuni Fudoki|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11481687}}" about {{ill|Mount Tsukuba|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mount Tsukuba|qq=}} (筑波山) and the folk tales about {{ill|Kūkai|4=en|6=fr|8=ja|9=弘法大師|10=simple|11=User:Immanuelle/Kūkai|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kūkai|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 空海|1=Kūkai|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q222227}} (弘法大師). Since many shrine origin stories involve deities traveling to find their enshrinement locations, this is considered a typical motif of a "traveling deity."
The origin tradition of the "Former Ise" is derived from texts like the "{{ill|Kotai Jingu Gishiki|ja|皇太神宮儀式帳|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kotai Jingu Gishiki|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 延暦儀式帳|1=Enryaku Gishikichō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q109596938}}, {{ill|Toyuke Gū Gishiki|ja|止由気宮儀式帳|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Toyuke Gū Gishiki|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 延暦儀式帳|1=Enryaku Gishikichō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q109596938}}, {{ill|Kogo Shūi|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kogo Shūi|qq=}}, and [[Engishiki]]." Although it was previously said to involve around twenty locations, it now includes over sixty. These traditions are based on those transmitted to various shrines, and there are cases where nearby locations claim to be the traditional site, leaving the truth of these claims unclear.
==Oomoto== A Moto-Ise Shrine "North of {{ill|Ayabe, Kyoto|lt=Ayabe|en|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ayabe, Kyoto|qq=}}", {{ill|Amanoiwato Shrine|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Amanoiwato Shrine|qq=}} was used in a symbolic act by the religious group Oomoto to emphasize their spiritual authority and connection to Japan's ancient religious traditions. Specifically, members of Oomoto collected sacred elements—fire, water, and earth—from [[Izumo-taisha]] during a pilgrimage. They then combined these elements with water from Moto-Ise, a site revered as the original location of the Ise Shrine and associated with the goddess Amaterasu. By mixing these sacred substances, Oomoto was asserting a deep and direct link to the ancient and most sacred sites of Shinto, effectively positioning themselves as a leading advocate for Japan's traditional spiritual practices.<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=v44BEAAAQBAJ&dq=%22Moto+Ise%22&pg=PA62|title=Prophet Motive: Deguchi Onisaburō, Oomoto, and the Rise of New Religions in Imperial Japan|last=Stalker|first=Nancy K.|date=2007-10-31|publisher=University of Hawaii Press|isbn=978-0-8248-6404-0|language=en|qq=draft}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Nao Deguchi A Biography of the Foundress of Oomoto|url=https://www.oomoto.or.jp/English/enKyos/kaisoden/index.html|access-date=2024-05-05|website=www.oomoto.or.jp}}</ref> Their headquarters are near this "Moto-Ise"<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=xlG3F6gSm9UC&dq=%22Moto+Ise%22&pg=PA232|title=Historical Dictionary of Shinto|last=Picken|first=Stuart D. B.|date=2010-12-28|publisher=Scarecrow Press|isbn=978-0-8108-7372-8|language=en}}</ref>.

Edward|date=2007-02-28|publisher=University of Hawaii Press|isbn=978-0-8248-3035-9|language=en}}</ref> These shrines are subject to a large amount of historical research.<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=XEIiEAAAQBAJ&dq=%22Moto+Ise%22&pg=PA534|title=RLE: Japan Mini-Set F: Philosophy and Religion (4 vols)|last=Authors|first=Various|date=2021-03-18|publisher=Routledge|isbn=978-1-136-90356-4|language=en}}</ref>
== Hibara Shrine == '''Hibara Shrine''' is a subshrine of Omiwa Shrine at the foot of {{ill|10=en|11=Mount_Miwa|12=fr|13=Mont Miwa|Mount Miwa|lt=Mount Miwa|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/10=en|qq=}} in [[:en:Sakurai, Nara|Sakurai]], [[:en:Nara Prefecture|Nara Prefecture]]. The shrine is identified as the place where the {{ill|10=en|11=Yata-no-Kagami|Yata-no-Kagami|lt=Yata-no-Kagami|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/10=en|qq=}} and the {{ill|10=en|11=Kusanagi no Tsurugi|lt=Kusanagi-no-Tsurugi|Kusanagi no Tsurugi|lt=Kusanagi no Tsurugi|lt=Kusanagi-no-Tsurugi|lt=Kusanagi no Tsurugi|lt=Kusanagi-no-Tsurugi|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/10=en|qq=}} were first enshrined after they were removed from the imperial palace. It is the first of many {{ill|Moto-Ise Shrines|lt=Moto-Ise|ja|元伊勢|1=Moto-Ise Shrines|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Moto-Ise Shrines|13=User:Immanuelle/Moto-Ise Shrines|qq=}} shrines<ref name="greenshinto2">{{Cite web|last=D|first=John|date=2011-08-10|title=Hibara Jinja and Amaterasu|url=https://www.greenshinto.com/2011/08/11/hibara-jinja-and-amaterasu/|access-date=2023-10-18|website=Green Shinto|language=en-GB}}</ref>.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Hibara Jinja Shrine（Nara）|url=https://www.jldb.bunka.go.jp/en/location/290100006/?search=1&q=Hibara+Shrine|access-date=2023-10-03|website=Nationwide location database|language=en}}</ref><ref name="YAMATO UNKNOWN ORIGIN-2">{{Cite web|title=Omiwa Jinja Shrine/Sai Jinja Shrine/Kuehiko Jinja Shrine/Hibara Jinja Shrine│Destinations│Discover YAMATO│YAMATO UNKNOWN ORIGIN|url=http://www.city.sakurai.lg.jp/section/yamato-travel/destination/area01/spot02/|access-date=2023-10-03|website=YAMATO UNKNOWN ORIGIN|language=en}}</ref> Amaterasu was originally enshrined there before eventually moving to other Moto-Ise shrines and then finally to [[Ise Grand Shrine|Ise Jingu]].<ref name="YAMATO UNKNOWN ORIGIN-2" /> It has an [[Iwakura rock]] and a Shinza made of [[:en:Cleyera japonica|Cleyera japonica]] wood.<ref name="YAMATO UNKNOWN ORIGIN-2" />
It has a prominent unique closable triple [[torii]] gate.<ref name="greenshinto2" />
== Summary == The deity enshrined at the Inner Shrine (内宮) of Ise Jingu (伊勢神宮), [[Amaterasu|Amaterasu Omikami]] (天照大御神), is considered the [[Oyagami|ancestral deity]] (皇祖神) of the emperors. Up until the era of the 10th Emperor, [[:en:Emperor Sujin|Emperor Sujin]] (崇神天皇), it is said that the emperor and Amaterasu Omikami shared the same residence, known as "sharing the same bed and palace" (同床共殿). Initially, she was enshrined within the [[Tokyo Imperial Palace|Imperial Palace]] (皇居), but fearing this arrangement, the emperor entrusted her divine spirit to Princess {{ill|Toyosukiiri-hime|ja|豊鍬入姫命|en:draft|simple|User:Immanuelle/Toyosukiiri-hime|fr|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Toyosukiiri-hime|qq=}} (豊鋤入姫命)<ref name="iUniverse" />, who established a sacred fence known as the "Iseki-no-himorogi" (磯城の神籬) in Iseshiro, Kasafu village (笠縫邑), [[:en:Yamato Province|Yamato province]] (倭国). This began a search for an ideal location for her permanent enshrinement, which led to several relocations. Eventually, the 11th Emperor, [[:en:Emperor Suinin|Emperor Suijin]]'s (垂仁天皇) fourth princess, Princess [[:en:Yamatohime-no-mikoto|Yamatohime-no-mikoto]] (倭姫命), took over this mission, and after approximately 90 years, the shrine was moved to its current location.<ref name="iUniverse" /><ref name="Dougill-2023" /> The "Iseki-no-himorogi" is first mentioned during the relocation of Amaterasu Omikami to Yamato Kasafu village in the Chronicles of Emperor Suinin, where it is imagined as a facility for the placement of a {{ill|Mirrors in Shinto|lt=Mirrors in Shinto|lt=Shinto mirror|lt=divine mirror|simple|User:Immanuelle/Shinto mirror|en|Mirrors in Shinto|fr|Miroirs dans le shintoïsme|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinto mirror|qq=}}, symbolizing a sacred area akin to a rock seat, with a vast horizontal landscape preserving the tradition of the Iseshiro form. At Ise Jingu, the Shin-no-mihashira (心御柱), a central sacred pillar, is largely buried in the ground with its surroundings wrapped in sakaki (榊), and ritual pottery symbolizes the rituals. It is said that when the divine mirror of Amaterasu Omikami was first dedicated, a five-hundred-year-old tree from {{ill|Mount Amanokagu|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mount Amanokagu|qq=}} was dug up, with jewels hung on its upper branches and a mirror on its middle branches, but the sakaki-decorated Shin-no-mihashira symbolizes the appearance of this sacred tree during rituals. The relocation process is not mentioned in the "[[Kojiki]]," but is briefly noted in the "[[Nihon Shoki]]," more detailed in the "{{ill|Kotai Jingu Gishiki|ja|皇太神宮儀式帳|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kotai Jingu Gishiki|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 延暦儀式帳|1=Enryaku Gishikichō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q109596938}}," and most elaborately in the "{{ill|Yamatohime-no-mikoto Seiki|ja|倭姫命世記|1=Yamatohime no Mikoto Seiki|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yamatohime-no-mikoto Seiki|13=User:Immanuelle/Yamatohime no Mikoto Seiki|qq=}}," a medieval text from the "{{ill|Shintō Gobusho|lt=Shintō Gobusho|lt=Shinto Gobusho|ja|神道五部書|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinto Gobusho|qq=}} (神道五部書)."
The deity of the Outer Shrine (外宮), [[:en:Toyouke-hime|Toyouke-no-Ōmikami]] (豊受大御神), although not mentioned in the "[[Kojiki]]" or "[[Nihon Shoki]]," is said in the "{{ill|Toyuke Gū Gishiki|ja|止由気宮儀式帳|lt=Toyuke Shrine Ritual Book|lt_ja=止由気宮儀式帳|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Toyuke Gū Gishiki|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 延暦儀式帳|1=Enryaku Gishikichō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q109596938}}" and "{{ill|Yamatohime-no-mikoto Seiki|ja|倭姫命世記|lt=Yamatohime-no-mikoto Chronicles|lt_ja=倭姫命世記|1=Yamatohime no Mikoto Seiki|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yamatohime-no-mikoto Seiki|13=User:Immanuelle/Yamatohime no Mikoto Seiki|qq=}}" to have been relocated from Tango Province (丹後国) (now part of Tanba Province (丹波国)) to her current site by divine command of Amaterasu Omikami during the era of the 21st Emperor, Emperor Yūryaku (雄略天皇).
The tale of Amaterasu Omikami's wanderings is considered similar to the ancestral deity stories in the "{{ill|Hitachi Province Fudoki|ja|常陸国風土記|zh|常陸國風土記|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hitachi Province Fudoki|qq=|1=Hitachi no Kuni Fudoki|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11481687}}" about {{ill|Mount Tsukuba|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mount Tsukuba|qq=}} (筑波山) and the folk tales about {{ill|Kūkai|4=en|6=fr|8=ja|9=弘法大師|10=simple|11=User:Immanuelle/Kūkai|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kūkai|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 空海|1=Kūkai|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q222227}} (弘法大師). Since many shrine origin stories involve deities traveling to find their enshrinement locations, this is considered a typical motif of a "traveling deity."
The origin tradition of the "Former Ise" is derived from texts like the "{{ill|Kotai Jingu Gishiki|ja|皇太神宮儀式帳|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kotai Jingu Gishiki|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 延暦儀式帳|1=Enryaku Gishikichō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q109596938}}, {{ill|Toyuke Gū Gishiki|ja|止由気宮儀式帳|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Toyuke Gū Gishiki|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 延暦儀式帳|1=Enryaku Gishikichō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q109596938}}, {{ill|Kogo Shūi|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kogo Shūi|qq=}}, and [[Engishiki]]." Although it was previously said to involve around twenty locations, it now includes over sixty. These traditions are based on those transmitted to various shrines, and there are cases where nearby locations claim to be the traditional site, leaving the truth of these claims unclear.
==Oomoto== A Moto-Ise Shrine "North of {{ill|Ayabe, Kyoto|lt=Ayabe|en|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ayabe, Kyoto|qq=}}", {{ill|Amanoiwato Shrine|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Amanoiwato Shrine|qq=}} was used in a symbolic act by the religious group Oomoto to emphasize their spiritual authority and connection to Japan's ancient religious traditions. Specifically, members of Oomoto collected sacred elements—fire, water, and earth—from [[Izumo-taisha]] during a pilgrimage. They then combined these elements with water from Moto-Ise, a site revered as the original location of the Ise Shrine and associated with the goddess Amaterasu. By mixing these sacred substances, Oomoto was asserting a deep and direct link to the ancient and most sacred sites of Shinto, effectively positioning themselves as a leading advocate for Japan's traditional spiritual practices.<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=v44BEAAAQBAJ&dq=%22Moto+Ise%22&pg=PA62|title=Prophet Motive: Deguchi Onisaburō, Oomoto, and the Rise of New Religions in Imperial Japan|last=Stalker|first=Nancy K.|date=2007-10-31|publisher=University of Hawaii Press|isbn=978-0-8248-6404-0|language=en|qq=draft}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Nao Deguchi A Biography of the Foundress of Oomoto|url=https://www.oomoto.or.jp/English/enKyos/kaisoden/index.html|access-date=2024-05-05|website=www.oomoto.or.jp}}</ref> Their headquarters are near this "Moto-Ise"<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=xlG3F6gSm9UC&dq=%22Moto+Ise%22&pg=PA232|title=Historical Dictionary of Shinto|last=Picken|first=Stuart D. B.|date=2010-12-28|publisher=Scarecrow Press|isbn=978-0-8108-7372-8|language=en}}</ref>.

Edward |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=7pEOicqsjv0C&dq=%22Moto-Ise%22&pg=PA201 |title=Himiko and Japan's Elusive Chiefdom of Yamatai: Archaeology, History, and Mythology |date=2007-02-28 |publisher=University of Hawaii Press |isbn=978-0-8248-3035-9 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Stalker |first=Nancy K. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=v44BEAAAQBAJ&dq=%22Moto-Ise%22&pg=PA62 |title=Prophet Motive: Deguchi Onisaburō, Oomoto, and the Rise of New Religions in Imperial Japan |date=2007-10-31 |publisher=University of Hawaii Press |isbn=978-0-8248-6404-0 |language=en}}</ref><ref name="iUniverse">{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=nPaezHFlfNQC&dq=%22Moto+Ise%22&pg=PT107|title=Where the Trees Grow Thick|publisher=iUniverse|isbn=978-0-595-28240-1|language=en}}</ref><ref name="Göttler-2017">{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=uyk_DwAAQBAJ&dq=%22Moto+Ise%22&pg=PA437|title=The Nomadic Object: The Challenge of World for Early Modern Religious Art|last1=Göttler|first1=Christine|last2=Mochizuki|first2=Mia|date=2017-11-06|publisher=BRILL|isbn=978-90-04-35450-0|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=PvgsAAAAIAAJ&dq=%22Moto+Ise%22&pg=RA3-PA147|title=Pamphlet - Dept. of the Army|last=Army|first=United States Department of the|date=1945|publisher=Headquarters, Department of the Army.|language=en}}</ref><ref name="Dougill-2023">{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=-H_cEAAAQBAJ&dq=%22Moto+Ise%22&pg=PT204|title=Off the Beaten Tracks in Japan: A Journey by Train from Hokkaido to Kyushu|last=Dougill|first=John|date=2023-11-07|publisher=Stone Bridge Press, Inc.|isbn=978-1-61172-963-4|language=en}}</ref> The first one was [[:en:Ōmiwa Shrine|Hibara Shrine]] (a subshrine of [[:en:Ōmiwa Shrine|Ōmiwa Shrine]]).<ref name="greenshinto">{{Cite web |last=D |first=John |date=2011-08-10 |title=Hibara Jinja and Amaterasu |url=https://www.greenshinto.com/2011/08/11/hibara-jinja-and-amaterasu/ |access-date=2023-10-18 |website=Green Shinto |language=en-GB}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Hibara Jinja Shrine（Nara） |url=https://www.jldb.bunka.go.jp/en/location/290100006/?search=1&q=Hibara+Shrine |access-date=2023-10-03 |website=Nationwide location database |language=en}}</ref><ref name="YAMATO UNKNOWN ORIGIN">{{Cite web |title=Omiwa Jinja Shrine/Sai Jinja Shrine/Kuehiko Jinja Shrine/Hibara Jinja Shrine│Destinations│Discover YAMATO│YAMATO UNKNOWN ORIGIN |url=http://www.city.sakurai.lg.jp/section/yamato-travel/destination/area01/spot02/ |access-date=2023-10-03 |website=YAMATO UNKNOWN ORIGIN |language=en}}</ref> Amaterasu was originally enshrined there before eventually moving to other Moto-Ise shrines and then finally to [[Ise Grand Shrine|Ise Jingu]].<ref name="YAMATO UNKNOWN ORIGIN" /><ref name="iUniverse" /><ref name="Göttler-2017" /><ref name="Dougill-2023" />
The journey was long so many shrines claim this title.<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=7pEOicqsjv0C&dq=%22Moto+Ise%22&pg=PA201|title=Himiko and Japan's Elusive Chiefdom of Yamatai: Archaeology, History, and Mythology|last=Kidder|first=J. Edward|date=2007-02-28|publisher=University of Hawaii Press|isbn=978-0-8248-3035-9|language=en}}</ref> These shrines are subject to a large amount of historical research.<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=XEIiEAAAQBAJ&dq=%22Moto+Ise%22&pg=PA534|title=RLE: Japan Mini-Set F: Philosophy and Religion (4 vols)|last=Authors|first=Various|date=2021-03-18|publisher=Routledge|isbn=978-1-136-90356-4|language=en}}</ref>
== Hibara Shrine == '''Hibara Shrine''' is a subshrine of Omiwa Shrine at the foot of {{ill|10=en|11=Mount_Miwa|12=fr|13=Mont Miwa|Mount Miwa|lt=Mount Miwa|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/10=en|qq=}} in [[:en:Sakurai, Nara|Sakurai]], [[:en:Nara Prefecture|Nara Prefecture]]. The shrine is identified as the place where the {{ill|10=en|11=Yata-no-Kagami|Yata-no-Kagami|lt=Yata-no-Kagami|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/10=en|qq=}} and the {{ill|10=en|11=Kusanagi no Tsurugi|lt=Kusanagi-no-Tsurugi|Kusanagi no Tsurugi|lt=Kusanagi no Tsurugi|lt=Kusanagi-no-Tsurugi|lt=Kusanagi no Tsurugi|lt=Kusanagi-no-Tsurugi|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/10=en|qq=}} were first enshrined after they were removed from the imperial palace. It is the first of many {{ill|Moto-Ise Shrines|lt=Moto-Ise|ja|元伊勢|1=Moto-Ise Shrines|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Moto-Ise Shrines|13=User:Immanuelle/Moto-Ise Shrines|qq=}} shrines<ref name="greenshinto2">{{Cite web|last=D|first=John|date=2011-08-10|title=Hibara Jinja and Amaterasu|url=https://www.greenshinto.com/2011/08/11/hibara-jinja-and-amaterasu/|access-date=2023-10-18|website=Green Shinto|language=en-GB}}</ref>.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Hibara Jinja Shrine（Nara）|url=https://www.jldb.bunka.go.jp/en/location/290100006/?search=1&q=Hibara+Shrine|access-date=2023-10-03|website=Nationwide location database|language=en}}</ref><ref name="YAMATO UNKNOWN ORIGIN-2">{{Cite web|title=Omiwa Jinja Shrine/Sai Jinja Shrine/Kuehiko Jinja Shrine/Hibara Jinja Shrine│Destinations│Discover YAMATO│YAMATO UNKNOWN ORIGIN|url=http://www.city.sakurai.lg.jp/section/yamato-travel/destination/area01/spot02/|access-date=2023-10-03|website=YAMATO UNKNOWN ORIGIN|language=en}}</ref> Amaterasu was originally enshrined there before eventually moving to other Moto-Ise shrines and then finally to [[Ise Grand Shrine|Ise Jingu]].<ref name="YAMATO UNKNOWN ORIGIN-2" /> It has an [[Iwakura rock]] and a Shinza made of [[:en:Cleyera japonica|Cleyera japonica]] wood.<ref name="YAMATO UNKNOWN ORIGIN-2" />
It has a prominent unique closable triple [[torii]] gate.<ref name="greenshinto2" />
== Summary == The deity enshrined at the Inner Shrine (内宮) of Ise Jingu (伊勢神宮), [[Amaterasu|Amaterasu Omikami]] (天照大御神), is considered the [[Oyagami|ancestral deity]] (皇祖神) of the emperors. Up until the era of the 10th Emperor, [[:en:Emperor Sujin|Emperor Sujin]] (崇神天皇), it is said that the emperor and Amaterasu Omikami shared the same residence, known as "sharing the same bed and palace" (同床共殿). Initially, she was enshrined within the [[Tokyo Imperial Palace|Imperial Palace]] (皇居), but fearing this arrangement, the emperor entrusted her divine spirit to Princess {{ill|Toyosukiiri-hime|ja|豊鍬入姫命|en:draft|simple|User:Immanuelle/Toyosukiiri-hime|fr|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Toyosukiiri-hime|qq=}} (豊鋤入姫命)<ref name="iUniverse" />, who established a sacred fence known as the "Iseki-no-himorogi" (磯城の神籬) in Iseshiro, Kasafu village (笠縫邑), [[:en:Yamato Province|Yamato province]] (倭国). This began a search for an ideal location for her permanent enshrinement, which led to several relocations. Eventually, the 11th Emperor, [[:en:Emperor Suinin|Emperor Suijin]]'s (垂仁天皇) fourth princess, Princess [[:en:Yamatohime-no-mikoto|Yamatohime-no-mikoto]] (倭姫命), took over this mission, and after approximately 90 years, the shrine was moved to its current location.<ref name="iUniverse" /><ref name="Dougill-2023" /> The "Iseki-no-himorogi" is first mentioned during the relocation of Amaterasu Omikami to Yamato Kasafu village in the Chronicles of Emperor Suinin, where it is imagined as a facility for the placement of a {{ill|Mirrors in Shinto|lt=Mirrors in Shinto|lt=Shinto mirror|lt=divine mirror|simple|User:Immanuelle/Shinto mirror|en|Mirrors in Shinto|fr|Miroirs dans le shintoïsme|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinto mirror|qq=}}, symbolizing a sacred area akin to a rock seat, with a vast horizontal landscape preserving the tradition of the Iseshiro form. At Ise Jingu, the Shin-no-mihashira (心御柱), a central sacred pillar, is largely buried in the ground with its surroundings wrapped in sakaki (榊), and ritual pottery symbolizes the rituals. It is said that when the divine mirror of Amaterasu Omikami was first dedicated, a five-hundred-year-old tree from {{ill|Mount Amanokagu|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mount Amanokagu|qq=}} was dug up, with jewels hung on its upper branches and a mirror on its middle branches, but the sakaki-decorated Shin-no-mihashira symbolizes the appearance of this sacred tree during rituals. The relocation process is not mentioned in the "[[Kojiki]]," but is briefly noted in the "[[Nihon Shoki]]," more detailed in the "{{ill|Kotai Jingu Gishiki|ja|皇太神宮儀式帳|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kotai Jingu Gishiki|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 延暦儀式帳|1=Enryaku Gishikichō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q109596938}}," and most elaborately in the "{{ill|Yamatohime-no-mikoto Seiki|ja|倭姫命世記|1=Yamatohime no Mikoto Seiki|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yamatohime-no-mikoto Seiki|13=User:Immanuelle/Yamatohime no Mikoto Seiki|qq=}}," a medieval text from the "{{ill|Shintō Gobusho|lt=Shintō Gobusho|lt=Shinto Gobusho|ja|神道五部書|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinto Gobusho|qq=}} (神道五部書)."
The deity of the Outer Shrine (外宮), [[:en:Toyouke-hime|Toyouke-no-Ōmikami]] (豊受大御神), although not mentioned in the "[[Kojiki]]" or "[[Nihon Shoki]]," is said in the "{{ill|Toyuke Gū Gishiki|ja|止由気宮儀式帳|lt=Toyuke Shrine Ritual Book|lt_ja=止由気宮儀式帳|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Toyuke Gū Gishiki|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 延暦儀式帳|1=Enryaku Gishikichō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q109596938}}" and "{{ill|Yamatohime-no-mikoto Seiki|ja|倭姫命世記|lt=Yamatohime-no-mikoto Chronicles|lt_ja=倭姫命世記|1=Yamatohime no Mikoto Seiki|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yamatohime-no-mikoto Seiki|13=User:Immanuelle/Yamatohime no Mikoto Seiki|qq=}}" to have been relocated from Tango Province (丹後国) (now part of Tanba Province (丹波国)) to her current site by divine command of Amaterasu Omikami during the era of the 21st Emperor, Emperor Yūryaku (雄略天皇).
The tale of Amaterasu Omikami's wanderings is considered similar to the ancestral deity stories in the "{{ill|Hitachi Province Fudoki|ja|常陸国風土記|zh|常陸國風土記|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hitachi Province Fudoki|qq=|1=Hitachi no Kuni Fudoki|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11481687}}" about {{ill|Mount Tsukuba|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mount Tsukuba|qq=}} (筑波山) and the folk tales about {{ill|Kūkai|4=en|6=fr|8=ja|9=弘法大師|10=simple|11=User:Immanuelle/Kūkai|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kūkai|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 空海|1=Kūkai|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q222227}} (弘法大師). Since many shrine origin stories involve deities traveling to find their enshrinement locations, this is considered a typical motif of a "traveling deity."
The origin tradition of the "Former Ise" is derived from texts like the "{{ill|Kotai Jingu Gishiki|ja|皇太神宮儀式帳|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kotai Jingu Gishiki|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 延暦儀式帳|1=Enryaku Gishikichō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q109596938}}, {{ill|Toyuke Gū Gishiki|ja|止由気宮儀式帳|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Toyuke Gū Gishiki|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 延暦儀式帳|1=Enryaku Gishikichō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q109596938}}, {{ill|Kogo Shūi|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kogo Shūi|qq=}}, and [[Engishiki]]." Although it was previously said to involve around twenty locations, it now includes over sixty. These traditions are based on those transmitted to various shrines, and there are cases where nearby locations claim to be the traditional site, leaving the truth of these claims unclear.
==Oomoto== A Moto-Ise Shrine "North of {{ill|Ayabe, Kyoto|lt=Ayabe|en|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ayabe, Kyoto|qq=}}", {{ill|Amanoiwato Shrine|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Amanoiwato Shrine|qq=}} was used in a symbolic act by the religious group Oomoto to emphasize their spiritual authority and connection to Japan's ancient religious traditions. Specifically, members of Oomoto collected sacred elements—fire, water, and earth—from [[Izumo-taisha]] during a pilgrimage. They then combined these elements with water from Moto-Ise, a site revered as the original location of the Ise Shrine and associated with the goddess Amaterasu. By mixing these sacred substances, Oomoto was asserting a deep and direct link to the ancient and most sacred sites of Shinto, effectively positioning themselves as a leading advocate for Japan's traditional spiritual practices.<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=v44BEAAAQBAJ&dq=%22Moto+Ise%22&pg=PA62|title=Prophet Motive: Deguchi Onisaburō, Oomoto, and the Rise of New Religions in Imperial Japan|last=Stalker|first=Nancy K.|date=2007-10-31|publisher=University of Hawaii Press|isbn=978-0-8248-6404-0|language=en|qq=draft}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Nao Deguchi A Biography of the Foundress of Oomoto|url=https://www.oomoto.or.jp/English/enKyos/kaisoden/index.html|access-date=2024-05-05|website=www.oomoto.or.jp}}</ref> Their headquarters are near this "Moto-Ise"<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=xlG3F6gSm9UC&dq=%22Moto+Ise%22&pg=PA232|title=Historical Dictionary of Shinto|last=Picken|first=Stuart D. B.|date=2010-12-28|publisher=Scarecrow Press|isbn=978-0-8108-7372-8|language=en}}</ref>.

== Hibara Shrine == '''Hibara Shrine''' is a subshrine of Omiwa Shrine at the foot of {{ill|10=en|11=Mount_Miwa|12=fr|13=Mont Miwa|Mount Miwa|lt=Mount Miwa|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/10=en|qq=}} in [[:en:Sakurai, Nara|Sakurai]], [[:en:Nara Prefecture|Nara Prefecture]]. The shrine is identified as the place where the {{ill|10=en|11=Yata-no-Kagami|Yata-no-Kagami|lt=Yata-no-Kagami|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/10=en|qq=}} and the {{ill|10=en|11=Kusanagi no Tsurugi|lt=Kusanagi-no-Tsurugi|Kusanagi no Tsurugi|lt=Kusanagi no Tsurugi|lt=Kusanagi-no-Tsurugi|lt=Kusanagi no Tsurugi|lt=Kusanagi-no-Tsurugi|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/10=en|qq=}} were first enshrined after they were removed from the imperial palace. It is the first of many {{ill|Moto-Ise Shrines|lt=Moto-Ise|ja|元伊勢|1=Moto-Ise Shrines|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Moto-Ise Shrines|13=User:Immanuelle/Moto-Ise Shrines|qq=}} shrines<ref name="greenshinto2">{{Cite web|last=D|first=John|date=2011-08-10|title=Hibara Jinja and Amaterasu|url=https://www.greenshinto.com/2011/08/11/hibara-jinja-and-amaterasu/|access-date=2023-10-18|website=Green Shinto|language=en-GB}}</ref>.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Hibara Jinja Shrine（Nara）|url=https://www.jldb.bunka.go.jp/en/location/290100006/?search=1&q=Hibara+Shrine|access-date=2023-10-03|website=Nationwide location database|language=en}}</ref><ref name="YAMATO UNKNOWN ORIGIN-2">{{Cite web|title=Omiwa Jinja Shrine/Sai Jinja Shrine/Kuehiko Jinja Shrine/Hibara Jinja Shrine│Destinations│Discover YAMATO│YAMATO UNKNOWN ORIGIN|url=http://www.city.sakurai.lg.jp/section/yamato-travel/destination/area01/spot02/|access-date=2023-10-03|website=YAMATO UNKNOWN ORIGIN|language=en}}</ref> Amaterasu was originally enshrined there before eventually moving to other Moto-Ise shrines and then finally to [[Ise Grand Shrine|Ise Jingu]].<ref name="YAMATO UNKNOWN ORIGIN-2" /> It has an [[Iwakura rock]] and a Shinza made of [[:en:Cleyera japonica|Cleyera japonica]] wood.<ref name="YAMATO UNKNOWN ORIGIN-2" />
It has a prominent unique closable triple [[torii]] gate.<ref name="greenshinto2" />
== Summary == The deity enshrined at the Inner Shrine (内宮) of Ise Jingu (伊勢神宮), [[Amaterasu|Amaterasu Omikami]] (天照大御神), is considered the [[Oyagami|ancestral deity]] (皇祖神) of the emperors. Up until the era of the 10th Emperor, [[:en:Emperor Sujin|Emperor Sujin]] (崇神天皇), it is said that the emperor and Amaterasu Omikami shared the same residence, known as "sharing the same bed and palace" (同床共殿). Initially, she was enshrined within the [[Tokyo Imperial Palace|Imperial Palace]] (皇居), but fearing this arrangement, the emperor entrusted her divine spirit to Princess {{ill|Toyosukiiri-hime|ja|豊鍬入姫命|en:draft|simple|User:Immanuelle/Toyosukiiri-hime|fr|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Toyosukiiri-hime|qq=}} (豊鋤入姫命)<ref name="iUniverse" />, who established a sacred fence known as the "Iseki-no-himorogi" (磯城の神籬) in Iseshiro, Kasafu village (笠縫邑), [[:en:Yamato Province|Yamato province]] (倭国). This began a search for an ideal location for her permanent enshrinement, which led to several relocations. Eventually, the 11th Emperor, [[:en:Emperor Suinin|Emperor Suijin]]'s (垂仁天皇) fourth princess, Princess [[:en:Yamatohime-no-mikoto|Yamatohime-no-mikoto]] (倭姫命), took over this mission, and after approximately 90 years, the shrine was moved to its current location.<ref name="iUniverse" /><ref name="Dougill-2023" /> The "Iseki-no-himorogi" is first mentioned during the relocation of Amaterasu Omikami to Yamato Kasafu village in the Chronicles of Emperor Suinin, where it is imagined as a facility for the placement of a {{ill|Mirrors in Shinto|lt=Mirrors in Shinto|lt=Shinto mirror|lt=divine mirror|simple|User:Immanuelle/Shinto mirror|en|Mirrors in Shinto|fr|Miroirs dans le shintoïsme|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinto mirror|qq=}}, symbolizing a sacred area akin to a rock seat, with a vast horizontal landscape preserving the tradition of the Iseshiro form. At Ise Jingu, the Shin-no-mihashira (心御柱), a central sacred pillar, is largely buried in the ground with its surroundings wrapped in sakaki (榊), and ritual pottery symbolizes the rituals. It is said that when the divine mirror of Amaterasu Omikami was first dedicated, a five-hundred-year-old tree from {{ill|Mount Amanokagu|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mount Amanokagu|qq=}} was dug up, with jewels hung on its upper branches and a mirror on its middle branches, but the sakaki-decorated Shin-no-mihashira symbolizes the appearance of this sacred tree during rituals. The relocation process is not mentioned in the "[[Kojiki]]," but is briefly noted in the "[[Nihon Shoki]]," more detailed in the "{{ill|Kotai Jingu Gishiki|ja|皇太神宮儀式帳|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kotai Jingu Gishiki|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 延暦儀式帳|1=Enryaku Gishikichō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q109596938}}," and most elaborately in the "{{ill|Yamatohime-no-mikoto Seiki|ja|倭姫命世記|1=Yamatohime no Mikoto Seiki|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yamatohime-no-mikoto Seiki|13=User:Immanuelle/Yamatohime no Mikoto Seiki|qq=}}," a medieval text from the "{{ill|Shintō Gobusho|lt=Shintō Gobusho|lt=Shinto Gobusho|ja|神道五部書|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinto Gobusho|qq=}} (神道五部書)."
The deity of the Outer Shrine (外宮), [[:en:Toyouke-hime|Toyouke-no-Ōmikami]] (豊受大御神), although not mentioned in the "[[Kojiki]]" or "[[Nihon Shoki]]," is said in the "{{ill|Toyuke Gū Gishiki|ja|止由気宮儀式帳|lt=Toyuke Shrine Ritual Book|lt_ja=止由気宮儀式帳|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Toyuke Gū Gishiki|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 延暦儀式帳|1=Enryaku Gishikichō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q109596938}}" and "{{ill|Yamatohime-no-mikoto Seiki|ja|倭姫命世記|lt=Yamatohime-no-mikoto Chronicles|lt_ja=倭姫命世記|1=Yamatohime no Mikoto Seiki|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yamatohime-no-mikoto Seiki|13=User:Immanuelle/Yamatohime no Mikoto Seiki|qq=}}" to have been relocated from Tango Province (丹後国) (now part of Tanba Province (丹波国)) to her current site by divine command of Amaterasu Omikami during the era of the 21st Emperor, Emperor Yūryaku (雄略天皇).
The tale of Amaterasu Omikami's wanderings is considered similar to the ancestral deity stories in the "{{ill|Hitachi Province Fudoki|ja|常陸国風土記|zh|常陸國風土記|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hitachi Province Fudoki|qq=|1=Hitachi no Kuni Fudoki|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11481687}}" about {{ill|Mount Tsukuba|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mount Tsukuba|qq=}} (筑波山) and the folk tales about {{ill|Kūkai|4=en|6=fr|8=ja|9=弘法大師|10=simple|11=User:Immanuelle/Kūkai|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kūkai|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 空海|1=Kūkai|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q222227}} (弘法大師). Since many shrine origin stories involve deities traveling to find their enshrinement locations, this is considered a typical motif of a "traveling deity."
The origin tradition of the "Former Ise" is derived from texts like the "{{ill|Kotai Jingu Gishiki|ja|皇太神宮儀式帳|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kotai Jingu Gishiki|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 延暦儀式帳|1=Enryaku Gishikichō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q109596938}}, {{ill|Toyuke Gū Gishiki|ja|止由気宮儀式帳|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Toyuke Gū Gishiki|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 延暦儀式帳|1=Enryaku Gishikichō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q109596938}}, {{ill|Kogo Shūi|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kogo Shūi|qq=}}, and [[Engishiki]]." Although it was previously said to involve around twenty locations, it now includes over sixty. These traditions are based on those transmitted to various shrines, and there are cases where nearby locations claim to be the traditional site, leaving the truth of these claims unclear.
==Oomoto== A Moto-Ise Shrine "North of {{ill|Ayabe, Kyoto|lt=Ayabe|en|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ayabe, Kyoto|qq=}}", {{ill|Amanoiwato Shrine|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Amanoiwato Shrine|qq=}} was used in a symbolic act by the religious group Oomoto to emphasize their spiritual authority and connection to Japan's ancient religious traditions. Specifically, members of Oomoto collected sacred elements—fire, water, and earth—from [[Izumo-taisha]] during a pilgrimage. They then combined these elements with water from Moto-Ise, a site revered as the original location of the Ise Shrine and associated with the goddess Amaterasu. By mixing these sacred substances, Oomoto was asserting a deep and direct link to the ancient and most sacred sites of Shinto, effectively positioning themselves as a leading advocate for Japan's traditional spiritual practices.<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=v44BEAAAQBAJ&dq=%22Moto+Ise%22&pg=PA62|title=Prophet Motive: Deguchi Onisaburō, Oomoto, and the Rise of New Religions in Imperial Japan|last=Stalker|first=Nancy K.|date=2007-10-31|publisher=University of Hawaii Press|isbn=978-0-8248-6404-0|language=en|qq=draft}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Nao Deguchi A Biography of the Foundress of Oomoto|url=https://www.oomoto.or.jp/English/enKyos/kaisoden/index.html|access-date=2024-05-05|website=www.oomoto.or.jp}}</ref> Their headquarters are near this "Moto-Ise"<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=xlG3F6gSm9UC&dq=%22Moto+Ise%22&pg=PA232|title=Historical Dictionary of Shinto|last=Picken|first=Stuart D. B.|date=2010-12-28|publisher=Scarecrow Press|isbn=978-0-8108-7372-8|language=en}}</ref>.

The journey was long so many shrines claim this title.<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=7pEOicqsjv0C&dq=%22Moto+Ise%22&pg=PA201|title=Himiko and Japan's Elusive Chiefdom of Yamatai: Archaeology, History, and Mythology|last=Kidder|first=J. Edward|date=2007-02-28|publisher=University of Hawaii Press|isbn=978-0-8248-3035-9|language=en}}</ref> These shrines are subject to a large amount of historical research.<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=XEIiEAAAQBAJ&dq=%22Moto+Ise%22&pg=PA534|title=RLE: Japan Mini-Set F: Philosophy and Religion (4 vols)|last=Authors|first=Various|date=2021-03-18|publisher=Routledge|isbn=978-1-136-90356-4|language=en}}</ref>
== Hibara Shrine == '''Hibara Shrine''' is a subshrine of Omiwa Shrine at the foot of {{ill|10=en|11=Mount_Miwa|12=fr|13=Mont Miwa|Mount Miwa|lt=Mount Miwa|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/10=en|qq=}} in [[:en:Sakurai, Nara|Sakurai]], [[:en:Nara Prefecture|Nara Prefecture]]. The shrine is identified as the place where the {{ill|10=en|11=Yata-no-Kagami|Yata-no-Kagami|lt=Yata-no-Kagami|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/10=en|qq=}} and the {{ill|10=en|11=Kusanagi no Tsurugi|lt=Kusanagi-no-Tsurugi|Kusanagi no Tsurugi|lt=Kusanagi no Tsurugi|lt=Kusanagi-no-Tsurugi|lt=Kusanagi no Tsurugi|lt=Kusanagi-no-Tsurugi|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/10=en|qq=}} were first enshrined after they were removed from the imperial palace. It is the first of many {{ill|Moto-Ise Shrines|lt=Moto-Ise|ja|元伊勢|1=Moto-Ise Shrines|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Moto-Ise Shrines|13=User:Immanuelle/Moto-Ise Shrines|qq=}} shrines<ref name="greenshinto2">{{Cite web|last=D|first=John|date=2011-08-10|title=Hibara Jinja and Amaterasu|url=https://www.greenshinto.com/2011/08/11/hibara-jinja-and-amaterasu/|access-date=2023-10-18|website=Green Shinto|language=en-GB}}</ref>.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Hibara Jinja Shrine（Nara）|url=https://www.jldb.bunka.go.jp/en/location/290100006/?search=1&q=Hibara+Shrine|access-date=2023-10-03|website=Nationwide location database|language=en}}</ref><ref name="YAMATO UNKNOWN ORIGIN-2">{{Cite web|title=Omiwa Jinja Shrine/Sai Jinja Shrine/Kuehiko Jinja Shrine/Hibara Jinja Shrine│Destinations│Discover YAMATO│YAMATO UNKNOWN ORIGIN|url=http://www.city.sakurai.lg.jp/section/yamato-travel/destination/area01/spot02/|access-date=2023-10-03|website=YAMATO UNKNOWN ORIGIN|language=en}}</ref> Amaterasu was originally enshrined there before eventually moving to other Moto-Ise shrines and then finally to [[Ise Grand Shrine|Ise Jingu]].<ref name="YAMATO UNKNOWN ORIGIN-2" /> It has an [[Iwakura rock]] and a Shinza made of [[:en:Cleyera japonica|Cleyera japonica]] wood.<ref name="YAMATO UNKNOWN ORIGIN-2" />
It has a prominent unique closable triple [[torii]] gate.<ref name="greenshinto2" />
== Summary == The deity enshrined at the Inner Shrine (内宮) of Ise Jingu (伊勢神宮), [[Amaterasu|Amaterasu Omikami]] (天照大御神), is considered the [[Oyagami|ancestral deity]] (皇祖神) of the emperors. Up until the era of the 10th Emperor, [[:en:Emperor Sujin|Emperor Sujin]] (崇神天皇), it is said that the emperor and Amaterasu Omikami shared the same residence, known as "sharing the same bed and palace" (同床共殿). Initially, she was enshrined within the [[Tokyo Imperial Palace|Imperial Palace]] (皇居), but fearing this arrangement, the emperor entrusted her divine spirit to Princess {{ill|Toyosukiiri-hime|ja|豊鍬入姫命|en:draft|simple|User:Immanuelle/Toyosukiiri-hime|fr|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Toyosukiiri-hime|qq=}} (豊鋤入姫命)<ref name="iUniverse" />, who established a sacred fence known as the "Iseki-no-himorogi" (磯城の神籬) in Iseshiro, Kasafu village (笠縫邑), [[:en:Yamato Province|Yamato province]] (倭国). This began a search for an ideal location for her permanent enshrinement, which led to several relocations. Eventually, the 11th Emperor, [[:en:Emperor Suinin|Emperor Suijin]]'s (垂仁天皇) fourth princess, Princess [[:en:Yamatohime-no-mikoto|Yamatohime-no-mikoto]] (倭姫命), took over this mission, and after approximately 90 years, the shrine was moved to its current location.<ref name="iUniverse" /><ref name="Dougill-2023" /> The "Iseki-no-himorogi" is first mentioned during the relocation of Amaterasu Omikami to Yamato Kasafu village in the Chronicles of Emperor Suinin, where it is imagined as a facility for the placement of a {{ill|Mirrors in Shinto|lt=Mirrors in Shinto|lt=Shinto mirror|lt=divine mirror|simple|User:Immanuelle/Shinto mirror|en|Mirrors in Shinto|fr|Miroirs dans le shintoïsme|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinto mirror|qq=}}, symbolizing a sacred area akin to a rock seat, with a vast horizontal landscape preserving the tradition of the Iseshiro form. At Ise Jingu, the Shin-no-mihashira (心御柱), a central sacred pillar, is largely buried in the ground with its surroundings wrapped in sakaki (榊), and ritual pottery symbolizes the rituals. It is said that when the divine mirror of Amaterasu Omikami was first dedicated, a five-hundred-year-old tree from {{ill|Mount Amanokagu|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mount Amanokagu|qq=}} was dug up, with jewels hung on its upper branches and a mirror on its middle branches, but the sakaki-decorated Shin-no-mihashira symbolizes the appearance of this sacred tree during rituals. The relocation process is not mentioned in the "[[Kojiki]]," but is briefly noted in the "[[Nihon Shoki]]," more detailed in the "{{ill|Kotai Jingu Gishiki|ja|皇太神宮儀式帳|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kotai Jingu Gishiki|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 延暦儀式帳|1=Enryaku Gishikichō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q109596938}}," and most elaborately in the "{{ill|Yamatohime-no-mikoto Seiki|ja|倭姫命世記|1=Yamatohime no Mikoto Seiki|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yamatohime-no-mikoto Seiki|13=User:Immanuelle/Yamatohime no Mikoto Seiki|qq=}}," a medieval text from the "{{ill|Shintō Gobusho|lt=Shintō Gobusho|lt=Shinto Gobusho|ja|神道五部書|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinto Gobusho|qq=}} (神道五部書)."
The deity of the Outer Shrine (外宮), [[:en:Toyouke-hime|Toyouke-no-Ōmikami]] (豊受大御神), although not mentioned in the "[[Kojiki]]" or "[[Nihon Shoki]]," is said in the "{{ill|Toyuke Gū Gishiki|ja|止由気宮儀式帳|lt=Toyuke Shrine Ritual Book|lt_ja=止由気宮儀式帳|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Toyuke Gū Gishiki|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 延暦儀式帳|1=Enryaku Gishikichō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q109596938}}" and "{{ill|Yamatohime-no-mikoto Seiki|ja|倭姫命世記|lt=Yamatohime-no-mikoto Chronicles|lt_ja=倭姫命世記|1=Yamatohime no Mikoto Seiki|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yamatohime-no-mikoto Seiki|13=User:Immanuelle/Yamatohime no Mikoto Seiki|qq=}}" to have been relocated from Tango Province (丹後国) (now part of Tanba Province (丹波国)) to her current site by divine command of Amaterasu Omikami during the era of the 21st Emperor, Emperor Yūryaku (雄略天皇).
The tale of Amaterasu Omikami's wanderings is considered similar to the ancestral deity stories in the "{{ill|Hitachi Province Fudoki|ja|常陸国風土記|zh|常陸國風土記|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hitachi Province Fudoki|qq=|1=Hitachi no Kuni Fudoki|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11481687}}" about {{ill|Mount Tsukuba|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mount Tsukuba|qq=}} (筑波山) and the folk tales about {{ill|Kūkai|4=en|6=fr|8=ja|9=弘法大師|10=simple|11=User:Immanuelle/Kūkai|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kūkai|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 空海|1=Kūkai|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q222227}} (弘法大師). Since many shrine origin stories involve deities traveling to find their enshrinement locations, this is considered a typical motif of a "traveling deity."
The origin tradition of the "Former Ise" is derived from texts like the "{{ill|Kotai Jingu Gishiki|ja|皇太神宮儀式帳|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kotai Jingu Gishiki|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 延暦儀式帳|1=Enryaku Gishikichō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q109596938}}, {{ill|Toyuke Gū Gishiki|ja|止由気宮儀式帳|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Toyuke Gū Gishiki|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 延暦儀式帳|1=Enryaku Gishikichō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q109596938}}, {{ill|Kogo Shūi|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kogo Shūi|qq=}}, and [[Engishiki]]." Although it was previously said to involve around twenty locations, it now includes over sixty. These traditions are based on those transmitted to various shrines, and there are cases where nearby locations claim to be the traditional site, leaving the truth of these claims unclear.
==Oomoto== A Moto-Ise Shrine "North of {{ill|Ayabe, Kyoto|lt=Ayabe|en|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ayabe, Kyoto|qq=}}", {{ill|Amanoiwato Shrine|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Amanoiwato Shrine|qq=}} was used in a symbolic act by the religious group Oomoto to emphasize their spiritual authority and connection to Japan's ancient religious traditions. Specifically, members of Oomoto collected sacred elements—fire, water, and earth—from [[Izumo-taisha]] during a pilgrimage. They then combined these elements with water from Moto-Ise, a site revered as the original location of the Ise Shrine and associated with the goddess Amaterasu. By mixing these sacred substances, Oomoto was asserting a deep and direct link to the ancient and most sacred sites of Shinto, effectively positioning themselves as a leading advocate for Japan's traditional spiritual practices.<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=v44BEAAAQBAJ&dq=%22Moto+Ise%22&pg=PA62|title=Prophet Motive: Deguchi Onisaburō, Oomoto, and the Rise of New Religions in Imperial Japan|last=Stalker|first=Nancy K.|date=2007-10-31|publisher=University of Hawaii Press|isbn=978-0-8248-6404-0|language=en|qq=draft}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Nao Deguchi A Biography of the Foundress of Oomoto|url=https://www.oomoto.or.jp/English/enKyos/kaisoden/index.html|access-date=2024-05-05|website=www.oomoto.or.jp}}</ref> Their headquarters are near this "Moto-Ise"<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=xlG3F6gSm9UC&dq=%22Moto+Ise%22&pg=PA232|title=Historical Dictionary of Shinto|last=Picken|first=Stuart D. B.|date=2010-12-28|publisher=Scarecrow Press|isbn=978-0-8108-7372-8|language=en}}</ref>.

The journey was long so many shrines claim this title.<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=7pEOicqsjv0C&dq=%22Moto+Ise%22&pg=PA201|title=Himiko and Japan's Elusive Chiefdom of Yamatai: Archaeology, History, and Mythology|last=Kidder|first=J. Edward|date=2007-02-28|publisher=University of Hawaii Press|isbn=978-0-8248-3035-9|language=en}}</ref> These shrines are subject to a large amount of historical research.<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=XEIiEAAAQBAJ&dq=%22Moto+Ise%22&pg=PA534|title=RLE: Japan Mini-Set F: Philosophy and Religion (4 vols)|last=Authors|first=Various|date=2021-03-18|publisher=Routledge|isbn=978-1-136-90356-4|language=en}}</ref>
== Hibara Shrine == '''Hibara Shrine''' is a subshrine of Omiwa Shrine at the foot of {{ill|10=en|11=Mount_Miwa|12=fr|13=Mont Miwa|Mount Miwa|lt=Mount Miwa|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/10=en|qq=}} in [[:en:Sakurai, Nara|Sakurai]], [[:en:Nara Prefecture|Nara Prefecture]]. The shrine is identified as the place where the {{ill|10=en|11=Yata-no-Kagami|Yata-no-Kagami|lt=Yata-no-Kagami|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/10=en|qq=}} and the {{ill|10=en|11=Kusanagi no Tsurugi|lt=Kusanagi-no-Tsurugi|Kusanagi no Tsurugi|lt=Kusanagi no Tsurugi|lt=Kusanagi-no-Tsurugi|lt=Kusanagi no Tsurugi|lt=Kusanagi-no-Tsurugi|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/10=en|qq=}} were first enshrined after they were removed from the imperial palace. It is the first of many {{ill|Moto-Ise Shrines|lt=Moto-Ise|ja|元伊勢|1=Moto-Ise Shrines|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Moto-Ise Shrines|13=User:Immanuelle/Moto-Ise Shrines|qq=}} shrines<ref name="greenshinto2">{{Cite web|last=D|first=John|date=2011-08-10|title=Hibara Jinja and Amaterasu|url=https://www.greenshinto.com/2011/08/11/hibara-jinja-and-amaterasu/|access-date=2023-10-18|website=Green Shinto|language=en-GB}}</ref>.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Hibara Jinja Shrine（Nara）|url=https://www.jldb.bunka.go.jp/en/location/290100006/?search=1&q=Hibara+Shrine|access-date=2023-10-03|website=Nationwide location database|language=en}}</ref><ref name="YAMATO UNKNOWN ORIGIN-2">{{Cite web|title=Omiwa Jinja Shrine/Sai Jinja Shrine/Kuehiko Jinja Shrine/Hibara Jinja Shrine│Destinations│Discover YAMATO│YAMATO UNKNOWN ORIGIN|url=http://www.city.sakurai.lg.jp/section/yamato-travel/destination/area01/spot02/|access-date=2023-10-03|website=YAMATO UNKNOWN ORIGIN|language=en}}</ref> Amaterasu was originally enshrined there before eventually moving to other Moto-Ise shrines and then finally to [[Ise Grand Shrine|Ise Jingu]].<ref name="YAMATO UNKNOWN ORIGIN-2" /> It has an [[Iwakura rock]] and a Shinza made of [[:en:Cleyera japonica|Cleyera japonica]] wood.<ref name="YAMATO UNKNOWN ORIGIN-2" />
It has a prominent unique closable triple [[torii]] gate.<ref name="greenshinto2" />
== Summary == The deity enshrined at the Inner Shrine (内宮) of Ise Jingu (伊勢神宮), [[Amaterasu|Amaterasu Omikami]] (天照大御神), is considered the [[Oyagami|ancestral deity]] (皇祖神) of the emperors. Up until the era of the 10th Emperor, [[:en:Emperor Sujin|Emperor Sujin]] (崇神天皇), it is said that the emperor and Amaterasu Omikami shared the same residence, known as "sharing the same bed and palace" (同床共殿). Initially, she was enshrined within the [[Tokyo Imperial Palace|Imperial Palace]] (皇居), but fearing this arrangement, the emperor entrusted her divine spirit to Princess {{ill|Toyosukiiri-hime|ja|豊鍬入姫命|en:draft|simple|User:Immanuelle/Toyosukiiri-hime|fr|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Toyosukiiri-hime|qq=}} (豊鋤入姫命)<ref name="iUniverse" />, who established a sacred fence known as the "Iseki-no-himorogi" (磯城の神籬) in Iseshiro, Kasafu village (笠縫邑), [[:en:Yamato Province|Yamato province]] (倭国). This began a search for an ideal location for her permanent enshrinement, which led to several relocations. Eventually, the 11th Emperor, [[:en:Emperor Suinin|Emperor Suijin]]'s (垂仁天皇) fourth princess, Princess [[:en:Yamatohime-no-mikoto|Yamatohime-no-mikoto]] (倭姫命), took over this mission, and after approximately 90 years, the shrine was moved to its current location.<ref name="iUniverse" /><ref name="Dougill-2023" /> The "Iseki-no-himorogi" is first mentioned during the relocation of Amaterasu Omikami to Yamato Kasafu village in the Chronicles of Emperor Suinin, where it is imagined as a facility for the placement of a {{ill|Mirrors in Shinto|lt=Mirrors in Shinto|lt=Shinto mirror|lt=divine mirror|simple|User:Immanuelle/Shinto mirror|en|Mirrors in Shinto|fr|Miroirs dans le shintoïsme|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinto mirror|qq=}}, symbolizing a sacred area akin to a rock seat, with a vast horizontal landscape preserving the tradition of the Iseshiro form. At Ise Jingu, the Shin-no-mihashira (心御柱), a central sacred pillar, is largely buried in the ground with its surroundings wrapped in sakaki (榊), and ritual pottery symbolizes the rituals. It is said that when the divine mirror of Amaterasu Omikami was first dedicated, a five-hundred-year-old tree from {{ill|Mount Amanokagu|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mount Amanokagu|qq=}} was dug up, with jewels hung on its upper branches and a mirror on its middle branches, but the sakaki-decorated Shin-no-mihashira symbolizes the appearance of this sacred tree during rituals. The relocation process is not mentioned in the "[[Kojiki]]," but is briefly noted in the "[[Nihon Shoki]]," more detailed in the "{{ill|Kotai Jingu Gishiki|ja|皇太神宮儀式帳|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kotai Jingu Gishiki|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 延暦儀式帳|1=Enryaku Gishikichō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q109596938}}," and most elaborately in the "{{ill|Yamatohime-no-mikoto Seiki|ja|倭姫命世記|1=Yamatohime no Mikoto Seiki|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yamatohime-no-mikoto Seiki|13=User:Immanuelle/Yamatohime no Mikoto Seiki|qq=}}," a medieval text from the "{{ill|Shintō Gobusho|lt=Shintō Gobusho|lt=Shinto Gobusho|ja|神道五部書|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinto Gobusho|qq=}} (神道五部書)."
The deity of the Outer Shrine (外宮), [[:en:Toyouke-hime|Toyouke-no-Ōmikami]] (豊受大御神), although not mentioned in the "[[Kojiki]]" or "[[Nihon Shoki]]," is said in the "{{ill|Toyuke Gū Gishiki|ja|止由気宮儀式帳|lt=Toyuke Shrine Ritual Book|lt_ja=止由気宮儀式帳|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Toyuke Gū Gishiki|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 延暦儀式帳|1=Enryaku Gishikichō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q109596938}}" and "{{ill|Yamatohime-no-mikoto Seiki|ja|倭姫命世記|lt=Yamatohime-no-mikoto Chronicles|lt_ja=倭姫命世記|1=Yamatohime no Mikoto Seiki|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yamatohime-no-mikoto Seiki|13=User:Immanuelle/Yamatohime no Mikoto Seiki|qq=}}" to have been relocated from Tango Province (丹後国) (now part of Tanba Province (丹波国)) to her current site by divine command of Amaterasu Omikami during the era of the 21st Emperor, Emperor Yūryaku (雄略天皇).
The tale of Amaterasu Omikami's wanderings is considered similar to the ancestral deity stories in the "{{ill|Hitachi Province Fudoki|ja|常陸国風土記|zh|常陸國風土記|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hitachi Province Fudoki|1=Hitachi no Kuni Fudoki|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11481687}}" about {{ill|Mount Tsukuba|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mount Tsukuba|qq=}} (筑波山) and the folk tales about {{ill|Kūkai|4=en|6=fr|8=ja|9=弘法大師|10=simple|11=User:Immanuelle/Kūkai|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kūkai|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 空海|1=Kūkai|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q222227}} (弘法大師). Since many shrine origin stories involve deities traveling to find their enshrinement locations, this is considered a typical motif of a "traveling deity."
The origin tradition of the "Former Ise" is derived from texts like the "{{ill|Kotai Jingu Gishiki|ja|皇太神宮儀式帳|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kotai Jingu Gishiki|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 延暦儀式帳|1=Enryaku Gishikichō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q109596938}}, {{ill|Toyuke Gū Gishiki|ja|止由気宮儀式帳|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Toyuke Gū Gishiki|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 延暦儀式帳|1=Enryaku Gishikichō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q109596938}}, {{ill|Kogo Shūi|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kogo Shūi|qq=}}, and [[Engishiki]]." Although it was previously said to involve around twenty locations, it now includes over sixty. These traditions are based on those transmitted to various shrines, and there are cases where nearby locations claim to be the traditional site, leaving the truth of these claims unclear.
==Oomoto== A Moto-Ise Shrine "North of {{ill|Ayabe, Kyoto|lt=Ayabe|en|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ayabe, Kyoto|qq=}}", {{ill|Amanoiwato Shrine|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Amanoiwato Shrine|qq=}} was used in a symbolic act by the religious group Oomoto to emphasize their spiritual authority and connection to Japan's ancient religious traditions. Specifically, members of Oomoto collected sacred elements—fire, water, and earth—from [[Izumo-taisha]] during a pilgrimage. They then combined these elements with water from Moto-Ise, a site revered as the original location of the Ise Shrine and associated with the goddess Amaterasu. By mixing these sacred substances, Oomoto was asserting a deep and direct link to the ancient and most sacred sites of Shinto, effectively positioning themselves as a leading advocate for Japan's traditional spiritual practices.<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=v44BEAAAQBAJ&dq=%22Moto+Ise%22&pg=PA62|title=Prophet Motive: Deguchi Onisaburō, Oomoto, and the Rise of New Religions in Imperial Japan|last=Stalker|first=Nancy K.|date=2007-10-31|publisher=University of Hawaii Press|isbn=978-0-8248-6404-0|language=en|qq=draft}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Nao Deguchi A Biography of the Foundress of Oomoto|url=https://www.oomoto.or.jp/English/enKyos/kaisoden/index.html|access-date=2024-05-05|website=www.oomoto.or.jp}}</ref> Their headquarters are near this "Moto-Ise"<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=xlG3F6gSm9UC&dq=%22Moto+Ise%22&pg=PA232|title=Historical Dictionary of Shinto|last=Picken|first=Stuart D. B.|date=2010-12-28|publisher=Scarecrow Press|isbn=978-0-8108-7372-8|language=en}}</ref>.
